#1146. Cucho Hernández heads both goals as Betis win 2-0 at Slovan Bratislava to go fourth

Two headers from Cucho Hernández gave Real Betis victory over Slovan Bratislava in the Champions League. The result strengthens Manuel Pellegrini's side's position in the league phase with three rounds left.

For Hernández, Tuesday night was his first start after more than a month out injured, and he marked it with a double in Bratislava. The win came in the fifth round of the Champions League league stage.

Ángel Ortiz supplied the cross for the opener, delivering it from the right for Hernández to meet at the back post. Isco then supplied the assist for his second after the break. That goal was his third of Betis’s Champions League campaign.

Hernández went off after 63 minutes, and Troy Parrott took his place. Marc Roca replaced Facundo Bernal, who had been booked in the seventh minute. Álvaro Fidalgo came on for Isco.

Pellegrini made six changes from the side that drew 1-1 with Sevilla in the derby. Isco, Abde and Antony kept their places.

The visitors dominated the game in every department. Betis completed 605 of their 670 passes, an accuracy of 90%. Slovan managed 309 passes in total. Betis put six shots on target, while Slovan managed two. The expected goals figure was 1.52 for Betis and 0.43 for the hosts.

Slovan goalkeeper Dominik Takáč made four saves. At the other end, Álvaro Vallés made a sharp save to stop Andraž Šporar, a moment UEFA’s match summary named as one of the key moments of the game. French referee Jérôme Brisard showed one yellow card to each side.

The game also brought Slovan coach Yaya Touré up against Pellegrini, his old manager at Manchester City. Touré’s side stay bottom of the table after five defeats. They have conceded 19 goals and scored only one.

Betis now have four wins and one defeat from five matches. They are well placed to fight for a top-eight finish over the last three rounds, according to AFP. A place in the top eight would send them straight into the last 16 without a play-off.

The remaining fixtures are demanding. Betis host Como on 9 December 2026 and Arsenal on 20 January 2027. They finish the league phase away to Bayern Munich on 27 January 2027.

¡¡FINAL EN BRATISLAVA!! ¡¡LA VICTORIA ES NUESTRA, EQUIPO! 🇸🇰🔝

¡Vamos, BETIS! 💚#DíaDeBetis #EuroBetis pic.twitter.com/So3QTJbA0L

— Real Betis Balompié 🌴💚 (@RealBetis) November 24, 2026

The result also continues a solid run in all competitions. Before the derby draw, Betis had beaten Elche 2-0 and Navalcarnero 3-2.

Attention now turns to LaLiga. Betis host Rayo Vallecano on Saturday 28 November.

#1145. 'Never Again!': Holocaust remembrance under pressure

Only a few Holocaust survivors remain who can share their stories firsthand. Meanwhile, voices calling for an end to what they describe as a "cult of guilt" are growing louder. How can Holocaust remembrance survive?

Young people pose inside a crematorium oven at the Buchenwald concentration camp memorial, laughing while they give the Nazi salute and take pictures of each other. "In a sense, they're trophies to post on social media for them to boast about — breaking the ultimate taboo," Jens-Christian Wagner, director of the Buchenwald and Mittelbau-Dora Memorials Foundation, told DW.

"Incidents like this have become more frequent in recent years. We have seen memorial trees planted in honor of concentration camp victims cut down. When something like this happens — and it happens regularly — I find it particularly despicable because, because it ultimately kills these people a second time," added Wagner.

Wagner is part of the curatorial team behind the exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in Bonn's Bundeskunsthalle, or the Art and Exhibition Hall of the Federal Republic of Germany. Wagner said Holocaust remembrance is under pressure, and the subject of intensifying attacks.

Critics have dismissed remembrance as a "cult of guilt" or "national masochism." With right-wing populism on the rise and historical revisionism becoming more common, Wagner worries about how Germany will remember the victims murdered by the Nazi regime. He is also concerned about the future of democracy. And soon, there will be no Holocaust survivors left to tell the true story of what happened.

This new exhibition tackles this concern head-on with numerous works of art and historical artifacts.

"I hope that perhaps even some people who don't already believe it's important to confront Nazi crimes will find their way to the exhibition," Wagner said. Memorial sites also attract visitors who aren't necessarily convinced of the need to confront these parts of history. Many of them are students.

"Let's not kid ourselves: When a teacher says 'We're going there,' it's always a mandatory visit," he said.

For today's young people, the Nazi era seems like the distant past, Wagner explained. "When you tell them to remember something that their grandparents didn't even experience, it naturally feels like an emotional burden. They can practically see the finger being wagged at them, and that doesn't exactly encourage learning."

A two-hour lecture won't have much of an impact if pupils aren't even paying attention. Instead, Buchenwald organizes full-day programs that allow students to explore historical sources together and make sense of history for themselves.

The next step, Wagner said, is to show young people that this chapter of history isn't closed. Visitors are encouraged to make connections between the past and current events like migration, for example.

"For the longest time, people have been discussing migration almost exclusively in terms of threats to public safety and crime. This broadly marginalizes certain groups — a mechanism that also worked for National Socialism," he said.

Eva Umlauf, 83, knows firsthand what it means to experience exclusion in its most extreme form. She is a patron of the Bonn exhibition.

In November 1944, Umlauf was just 2 years old when she, her pregnant mother and her father were deported by the Nazis from the Novaky labor camp in Slovakia to Auschwitz-Birkenau, the notorious Nazi concentration and extermination camp. She was saved from the gas chambers by mere days; the Nazis stopped using the chambers as the Red Army advanced, hoping to hide evidence of their crimes.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The camp was liberated on January 27, 1945. Three months later, Umlauf's sister Nora was born. But her father, her mother's siblings and her grandparents were all murdered. Eva barely survived herself. She suffered from tuberculosis, rickets and whooping cough, as well as edema caused by starvation. "Forget about the child. She won't survive," a doctor told her mother. But he was wrong.

Her mother returned to what was then Czechoslovakia with her two daughters, settling in Trencin. Eva Umlauf has no conscious memories of Auschwitz, but she carries her family's trauma deep within her.

Her mother never talked about what happened. Even so, Eva knew from an early age that she was a survivor. Her family rarely mentioned the camp by name, but one sentence came up again and again: "They stayed there." Eva knew that meant "they" were dead. And then, there was the number tattooed onto her arm: A26959.

Her mother taught her daughters not to draw attention to their Jewish identity — antisemitism was widespread throughout Czechoslovakia at the time. The small family managed to avoid harassment.

Eva Umlauf wanted to become a pediatrician, so she studied medicine. In the 1960s, she met her future husband, Jakob, who had also survived the Holocaust. He was an architect, active in Munich's Jewish community. They married in 1966, and she moved to Germany. She could hardly have imagined that she would one day live in the country of the perpetrators. "I don't hate Germans," she said. "But I cannot forgive. How can you forgive the deaths of 6 million people?"

It wasn't until much later that she first spoke publicly about the horrors of her early childhood. In 2011, she delivered a commemorative speech in Auschwitz on the anniversary of the camp's liberation. Since 2025, she has served as chair of the International Auschwitz Committee. A heart attack in 2014 motivated her to write her first book. "I was in intensive care. I thought to myself: If I get out of here healthy, I'll write a book."

Her memoir, "The Number on Your Forearm is Blue Like Your Eyes," was first released in 2016. The English translation followed in 2024. Since its publication, hardly a day has passed without someone asking Eva Umlauf to share her story.

She is appalled by the disrespectful behavior of young people at former concentration camps and by growing ignorance about the Holocaust. Sometimes, people even ask if she's too old to have a tattoo. But she also recalls a young man on the Munich subway who noticed the number on her arm and told her: "I want to apologize to you for what my ancestors did to you."

Umlauf never imagined that antisemitism would once again become so widespread in Europe and the United States. Nor did she expect the rise of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

"I go into schools. I'm so overwhelmed by the number of requests asking for my availability. And yet, the AfD is growing faster than I can reach students. It makes me think all this work is for nothing," she told DW.

Germany must never again fall under a right-wing dictatorship, she stressed. "'Never again' sounds nice, but all I can say is: It's happening again! Wouldn't 'Here We Go Again: Never Again' make a good title for the exhibition?"

She also shared her message to young people in the exhibition catalog, "Never Again": "You are not responsible for the crimes of your grandparents and great-grandparents. But you are responsible for the future. […] You are the generation that will shape our world. Make it a place where everyone can grow up safely, regardless of their background, faith or skin color."

She continues: "You don't have to be perfect. You just have to stay alert. Take care of your country."

The exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in the Bundeskunsthalle in Bonn runs through May 2, 2027.

This article was originally written in German.

#1144. Villarreal take record away losing run to Prague, where Slavia are 23 games without a win

Villarreal visit Slavia Prague after seven straight Champions League away defeats, a record for a Spanish club. Their hosts have gone 23 games without a win in the competition, so one of the two runs must end today.

Villarreal face Slavia Prague in the Champions League today carrying a losing run that UEFA says is a record for a Spanish club. They have lost each of their last seven away games in the competition. Their hosts carry a burden of their own. Slavia have eight draws and 15 defeats in their last 23 Champions League games. That run equals the competition’s worst, set by Steaua București between 2006 and 2013.

One of the two sequences has to end. A Slavia win would end their drought. Any other result would stop Villarreal’s run of away defeats. Kick-off is at 17:45 GMT.

That single win was a 3-1 home victory over Napoli on 13 October. The rest of the league phase has gone badly. Villarreal lost 3-2 at Borussia Dortmund on 8 September and 4-3 at Liverpool on 20 October. PSG then won 6-0 at La Cerámica on 3 November.

That leaves Villarreal 29th with three points. Another defeat would leave them close to elimination with three games to play.

The defence is the clearest problem. Villarreal have not kept a clean sheet in any of those 15 games, a club record. None of their last 35 games in the Champions League proper has ended goalless.

Falling behind early has also been fatal. Villarreal have never won a Champions League game when trailing at half-time, with two draws and 13 defeats. On eight occasions they have gone into the interval losing on the road, and every one of those matches ended in defeat.

Nathan Saliba, Juan Foyth and Ilias Akhomach are all missing in Prague, EFE reported. Gerard Moreno trained before the game and could return.

Trpišovský has six draws and 12 defeats from his 19 Champions League matches, all in charge of Slavia. UEFA describes that as the longest winless run of any coach in the competition. Slavia have also never beaten a Spanish club from the group or league phase onwards, with two draws and four defeats. The two clubs have not met since their two games in 2017.

Villarreal coach Iñigo Pérez still expects a hard night. Speaking in Prague, he said no team in the Champions League is as aggressive as Slavia. He called the game “transcendental” for how the league phase plays out. He added that the city’s cold weather would not be an excuse.

Defender Sergi Cardona said the team must learn last season’s lesson. He expects the game to be extremely demanding.

#1143. How Leeds United turned into Champions League contenders: Insiders reveal the ways 'manager's dream' Ethan Ampadu drives standards on and off the pitch, a hidden tougher side to Daniel Farke - and the club's January transfer window strategy

Published: 07:04 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 10:46 EST, 27 November 2026

He may not realise it yet, but the key member of Leeds United’s ever-improving team might just become one of their next great managers.

Leeds have been deservedly praised for their impressive start to the season, which sees them a point away from the likely Champions League places ahead of Saturday’s clash with Coventry.

Boss Daniel Farke is re-establishing the club in the top flight. Dominic Calvert-Lewin has signed a new contract and is an England player again. Towering centre back Tarik Muharemovic looks the buy of the season. The 49ers Enterprises Group are shrewd and careful owners.

But what about the guy who knits it all together? Ethan Ampadu had played for six clubs in three countries before he joined Leeds in 2023 but now he has found his home. Nearly half of Ampadu’s senior appearances have been in a Leeds shirt.

Ampadu’s work on the pitch and his behaviour off it suggest a manager in the making. Team-mates turn to him instinctively during matches and off the field, too, he makes Leeds tick.

‘I don’t know what Ethan’s plans are when he's finished playing but he has the stature and could offer a lot to the game beyond his playing career,’ says Stuart Dallas, who helped Leeds return to the Premier League in 2020 during an outstanding nine-year career at Elland Road.

Here Daily Mail Sport looks at why Leeds are on the rise – starting with their inspirational captain.

Inspired by brilliant new signings including Tarik Muharemovic (left) and James Trafford, Leeds are on the rise and in contention for the Champions League spots

Captain Ethan Ampadu makes Leeds tick on and off the pitch and is perceived as a manager in waiting

In the here and now, boss Daniel Farke is doing a superb job, having narrowly avoided being sacked in previous seasons

Though Dallas retired due to injury at the end of Ampadu’s first campaign at Leeds, he liked what he saw in those months.

‘I was at the training ground recently and the players had a later start – they were preparing for a Sunday game,’ Dallas, now a regular television pundit, tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘He was the first to turn up for the session. If you’re a young player coming through, it’s fantastic to see the captain setting that example.

‘He is an intelligent guy who takes responsibility. In his position you have to front up when things are not going well and protect people when they need it. He understands that.

‘A manager doesn’t want 20 different people knocking on his door. Ethan will take a lot of those minor problems away and I know how much of a privilege it is to him to captain Leeds.’

Ampadu takes the role extremely seriously. Daily Mail Sport understands he ensured Under-21 players who train regularly with the first team were included in the players' bonus pool. He also made sure they were listed as first-team squad members on the club website.

Ampadu wants the squad to feel like a family and will organise team bonding trips and meals out. Little things like that go a heck of a long way.

The club's leadership group comprises Ampadu, Calvert-Lewin, Jaka Bijol, Joe Rodon and James Justin – but third-choice goalkeeper Alex Cairns is another hugely respected figure in the squad.

Prolific striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin (pictured scoring in Leeds' 4-1 rout of Chelsea last weekend) has signed a new contract with the club

Calvert-Lewin (with Noah Okafor, right) is part of the team's leadership group, led by Ampadu

‘Ethan is a manager’s dream,’ explains former Leeds boss Simon Grayson, now a regular pundit on Leeds’ in-house TV channel LUTV. ‘Someone like that makes the manager’s job much less stressful.

‘If there’s an incident on or off the pitch, sometimes the captain can deal with it before it reaches the manager’s door. Ethan will do that. He has a level of respect from the other players so if he says something, it’s no different from Daniel Farke saying it.’

Farke is usually cautious when bringing back players from injury. When they are as important as Ampadu, though, he is prepared to make an exception.

The 26-year-old does not immediately catch the eye. He does not make spectacular passes or beat three opponents with a piece of skill. He has only three goals in 139 appearances.

Instead, he steps back into defence to cover the forward runs of Justin or Jayden Bogle. He makes sure he is in the right spot to stop counter-attacks. He is the one to notice when a team-mate has drifted out of position when defending a set-piece. Scouts see this and this is why Ampadu was considered by clubs in the so-called ‘Big Six’ before he signed a new four-year deal with Leeds last June.

‘He’ll go in and smash someone – fairly – if it’s a quiet game because it will wake the crowd up a bit,’ smiles Grayson. ‘You only realise how much you miss players like that when they are not in the team.’

Ampadu is just as popular with the fans. ‘As Leeds captains go, Gary McAllister and Lucas Radebe set a high bar when I was growing up,' says Rocco Dean of the Leeds, That! podcast. 'Although Ampadu has a little way to go, it's not inconceivable he could one day rank alongside those greats.'

At any time, there will usually be two or three players in a squad who are not popular with supporters. It is difficult to find them in the current Leeds side. ‘The players want to play for Leeds and it’s not just a "job",’ adds Mike Chard, who runs the All Leeds TV YouTube channel. ‘They don’t seem like a team. They seem like a family.’

‘As Leeds captains go, Gary McAllister and Lucas Radebe set a high bar when I was growing up... but Ampadu could one day rank alongside those greats'

Leeds have a broad agreement with Farke over a new contract and he deserves it. If Leeds beat Coventry, it will be his 80th win as boss in 162 games. Bielsa reached 80 in 163 matches.

In front of the cameras, Farke is open and affable – but he is no soft touch with his squad or coaches. The staff member who wore a snood over his head to training this week will be forced to don shorts and T-shirt for the remainder of the winter. His crime? Acting ‘big time’.

Footballers like to fool about when they are together but few would dare risk it when Farke is nearby. Daily Mail Sport has heard of one player who was acting the goat in the canteen and turned white when he realised he had failed to notice Farke entering the room.

Some bosses will encourage players to ask why they have been left out of the team. That is not typically the case with Farke. Generally, he makes his choices and then it falls to players to prove him wrong through their displays in training.

He can still forge close relationships with players, though. His rapport with Calvert-Lewin was a factor in the striker’s new deal and he has a similarly strong understanding with Noah Okafor.

Farke is probably as powerful now as he has ever been during his three-and-a-half seasons at Elland Road. At different points during his two Championship campaigns in charge, Farke was vulnerable to the sack. Even early last season, things looked a little dicey for him.

Switching to a back three in the 3-2 defeat at Manchester City last November turned it around for Leeds but this is about much more than a simple change of formation.

Despite his affable exterior and close bonds with certain players, Farke has a disciplinarian streak

Most of Leeds’ medical and conditioning team have been at Elland Road for more than a decade and unlike at many clubs, there is complete trust between them and Farke. The result? No injuries to first-team players as things stand.

On their instruction, Farke restricted Okafor to a 20-minute substitute appearance against Tottenham earlier this month. The Swiss attacker still scored the only goal.

In a typical week after a Saturday game, players will report to Thorp Arch for a recovery session on Sunday and have Monday off. Wednesday is usually the toughest day – gym in the morning followed by a training session, and more gym work in the afternoon.

Farke and his staff favour two particular possession drills: a four-a-side game with three ‘floating’ players who work with whoever has the ball, and a 10-a-side exercise with two floating players.

Brighton and Brentford have set the standard for recruitment in the last decade yet since promotion Leeds have not been far behind. Chairman Paraag Marathe has worked for global management consultants Bain, who rely heavily on data.

Led by sporting director Adam Underwood, Leeds do the same – though they mix art with science. New signings are shown videos of the celebrations in the city when Leeds were promoted in 2025. The current brief is to find physically robust, athletic players and unlike many clubs, Leeds are not obsessed with youth. The average age of their starting XI for the 4-1 win at Stamford Bridge was 27 years and 107 days. That figure has not dipped below 26 in any league game this season.

Underwood and his team anticipate a quiet January window in which no key players are expected to leave – dashing any hopes rivals may have had of stealing Muharemovic. The defender joined from Sassuolo for £30.1million last summer and his value is already much higher.

Under chairman Paraag Marathe (right), Leeds rely heavily on data in their recruitment. Their transfer track record has been excellent in recent years

The pinch point for the 49ers is coming. They aim to make Leeds worth £1billion by 2030. That will require significantly greater revenue: in 2024-25, when Leeds were promoted from the Championship, their revenue was £137m. That was a record for the second tier but they will likely need to exceed £300m in the coming years to hit the 49ers' £1bn target.

An expanded Elland Road should plug some of this gap when work is complete. Leeds are working on each stand in turn and hope the project will be finished by the end of 2030, giving them a 53,000 capacity.

Earlier this month, Leeds instructed US bank Allen & Co to seek additional investment, though it is thought a full sale is not currently on the cards.

Christian Purslow offers a different perspective. The former Aston Villa CEO, who also held senior positions at Liverpool and Chelsea, knows how tough it is for clubs outside the Big Six to break into that wealthy elite.

Speaking on The Football Boardcast, Purslow said: ‘If I were Paraag Marathe, I’d be looking at what’s gone on at some of my natural peers – Newcastle, Aston Villa, West Ham, Leicester, Everton. It’s so precarious when clubs like these try hard to push up against the so-called Big Six.

‘These guys (the 49ers) might conclude: "We’ve done our job, we’ve enjoyed the journey, let’s let someone else have the problem of competing with the Big Six in a world where Premier League and UEFA financial rules make it increasingly difficult." I would not rule that out in the next couple of years.’

‘They are allowed to dream big and enjoy themselves,’ Farke said of Leeds' supporters this week

Leeds are in no hurry. The sense at Elland Road is that the 49ers will not seek a shortcut by raising the wage bill or appointing a manager on a huge salary. They are prepared to go slow and steady.

As Purslow highlighted, if Newcastle – who have some of the world’s wealthiest owners – have accepted they cannot change the status quo, what chance does anyone else have?

After spending much of this century feeling gloomy, though, Leeds fans do not want to think about it too deeply.

‘They are allowed to dream big and enjoy themselves,’ Farke said this week. ‘After nearly three decades of suffering, it is a joy to bring this hope and belief back into the hearts, heads and souls of our supporters. This is why we are working so hard.’

#1142. Gordon double leads rotated Barcelona to 4-1 win in Baku without Lamine Yamal

Anthony Gordon scored twice as Hansi Flick's rotated Barcelona beat Sabah FK 4-1 in Baku without Lamine Yamal. The win lifts them to fourth in the Champions League league phase before Atlético Madrid and Manchester City visit.

In Baku, Barcelona completed the longest European away trip in their history and returned with a comfortable victory over Sabah FK. Hansi Flick rotated his side, and Lamine Yamal did not make the journey.

Joy-Lance Mickels scored a consolation goal for the Azerbaijani champions. Sabah had won only one of their first four league-phase matches. One of their defeats was a heavy loss to Manchester United.

The game was decided soon after the restart. Barcelona scored three times in the space of nine minutes. Gordon struck first, converting a rebound after Pokatilov saved from Jesus.

Four minutes later, Adeyemi finished Alejandro Balde’s cross. Jesus then made it four on the hour. He followed up after Jules Koundé’s header was saved.

The scoreline fits a side that controlled the ball for long spells.

The win also gave Flick room to manage his squad. Across 18 matches this season, Pedri had appeared every time, something no team-mate could match. He was taken off at half-time.

That decision had been agreed beforehand. Pedri was to play only the first 45 minutes whatever happened. Dani Olmo’s minutes were also limited to one half.

Resting key players in Baku could pay off over the coming fortnight. Barcelona are top of LaLiga and face two demanding fixtures at home.

The result keeps Barcelona on course for an automatic top-eight finish in the league phase. Manchester City sit eighth on 10 points. That makes the matchday 6 meeting a direct contest between two sides in the top eight.

Bournemouth came from behind to beat Celta Vigo 1-2 at the Municipal de Balaídos on Thursday 26 November 2026. With Javier Rueda García providing the assist for Aspas, Celta went into the break 1-0 up.

#1140. Newcastle fans turn on Jaissle as defeat triggers relegation concerns

Newcastle United did not just lose to Everton, they lost the home crowd, whose enthusiasm to back their team has drained from them at alarming speed.

This was a performance that belonged in the pre-takeover era, those bad old days under Steve McClaren, John Carver and Steve Bruce. It was a hugely satisfying evening for Everton manager David Moyes, who insisted there was “a way back” for Jack Grealish, even though he was once again left at home after he missed training last week without permission.

The atmosphere went flat early and gradually turned into anger and frustration. The crowd initially tried to stay with their team but were repeatedly punched in the face by the grim reality of the spectacle in front of them. They do not like the style of play, they do not like the application of the players and they cannot accept the results. They are fed up with pretending otherwise.

This was another miserable performance from Matthias Jaissle’s side, who did not manage a shot on target until the 86th minute. He has only been in the job three months, but nothing seems to be getting better.

“I have to take the responsibility,” he said. “We did not transfer the things we did in training. Hitting long balls all the time, that was not the plan. We were not brave enough to play short passes.

“As soon as the referee blew his whistle, the plan disappeared. We could feel the anger and the frustration, I felt it on the touchline. We are low on confidence and it shows.”

Newcastle looked listless, clueless and alarmingly devoid of belief in what they were being asked to do. They have the unmistakable whiff of a team in decline.

If they do not start playing a lot better, they will be worried about a relegation battle. It is four defeats in their last five games and the confidence in Jaissle to find solutions is fading. Rather than change what he is asking his team to do, he has doubled down on the formation and tactics.

Concerns have been creeping steadily upwards since August. There is a lack of confidence in the players, and worries about the quality of the eight new signings made over the summer.

In particular, there are serious misgivings about the implementation of the “vertical football” Jaissle has imported to the North East of England from the Austro-German Red Bull coaching school.

A night under the lights at St James’ Park should be a boisterous affair, but things went flat quickly. Newcastle, as they have tended to do this season, resorted to long balls punted forward. More often than not they were poorly directed – only 22 per cent were accurate over 98 minutes.

There was no fluency and no threat. The first groans were heard inside 15 minutes as another pass was hoisted harmlessly into the air. They grew more widespread and more frequent.

Everton, just as they had in their Carabao Cup win last week, looked comfortable. Recognising how easy it was to nullify Newcastle’s game plan, they offered an attacking threat of their own.

A rising shot from Merlin Röhl briefly had goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek worried. A free-kick into the Newcastle box caused panic. James Tarkowski won the first header, but Thierno Barry swung and missed with his left foot.

The groans began to turn into boos and whistles. Jaissle’s side could barely string more than two passes together. It felt precarious.

This is not an easy place to play football when the crowd airs its displeasure. As the first half limped on, there were players in black and white who looked like they could not handle the pressure.

It was a horrible game of football. With the last kick of the half, Everton should have taken the lead, Harrison Armstrong picked out Barry inside the box, but he made a mess of the finish. The referee’s whistle was accompanied by boos and a scream of “sort it out” from behind Jaissle’s technical area.

He did not follow those blunt instructions. Everton took the lead in such simple fashion and all Jaissle and his coaching staff could do was shake their heads at each other. Tyrique George was played in far too easily from a free-kick but his shot should have been saved by Hornicek. It was straight at the Czech, but it went through him and it left Barry with a tap in. Newcastle appealed for both a foul on Fabian Schar and an offside but got neither.

Newcastle and Everton meet for the second time in matter of days as the Premier League weekend concludes in the north east at St James’ Park. These teams encountered each other on Thursday night in the League Cup, where Everton won 3-1 at the Hill Dickinson to progress to the quarter-finals in that competition.

Newcastle, who won 2-0 at Crystal Palace in their last league outing, come into this game in 12th, with the chance to rise to seventh with a victory tonight. Their boss Matthias Jaissle has called on his players to use the defeat against Everton on Thursday as fuel for tonight.

“Now it is about taking that frustration into motivation for Monday and having that approach for the rematch,” Jaissle said. “We take it as a long-term journey, and our approach is to make progress, to see improvements. Now it is time to learn fast out of the mistakes that we just did. [There are] other phases where we can already see that we improved and this is something we can count on, we can build on, the good part. But football is also in the end about results so you need to avoid these simple mistakes.”

Everton, who have not won in the league since a 1-0 victory over Ipswich back in September, begin the night in 14th but, like Newcastle, could rise to seventh with a win. There are just two points that separate Bournemouth in seventh and Everton in 14th. Despite getting the better of Newcastle the other night, Everton manager David Moyes has warned that game will count for nothing tonight.

“It is a different ball game,” Moyes said. “Go to St James’ Park, on a Monday evening, they will get a crowd up there, you always know you are up against it. But we will go with confidence. We have played Newcastle a couple of times this year and done well, so we have to try and continue it. But Newcastle have got some really, really good players and players you have to concern yourself about.”

Jack Grealish was left out of Everton’s squad for that League Cup victory because of an unauthorised absence from training and the 31-year-old is not expected to be involved tonight.

These sides were involved in a dramatic fixture on this ground last season. Everton claimed a 3-2 victory, with Thierno Barry earning them all three points in the 83rd minute, moments after Jacob Murphy had equalised for Newcastle. Team news from St James’ Park to follow shortly.

#1139. Why Nvidia CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy matters for AI race

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has apologized for an affair with a woman the US believes was spying for China. The story could have profound implications for the world's most valuable company and the global AI race.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) company.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believe she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.

Nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It said in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."

"The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the company said Sunday. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information."

The company's shares fell in early trading on Monday.

While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.

"He's an honorable guy," said Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine."

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a company remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.

"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he said.

"His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this."

Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research company Radio Free Mobile, said the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he said.

"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the company is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO."

Nvidia and Huang's attitude toward China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

However, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-license review. China has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.

Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

However, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials. They fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost China's domestic AI sector, lead to its AI models catching up with the leading US models and see the chips being used in Chinese military applications.

The US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, if they're going to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.

Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

Windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the company. He also cast doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.

"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he said.

The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.

Nvidia's valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion company in October 2025.

However, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.

#1138. Europa Fight League! Marseille hooligans descend on Levski Sofia end after 'Nazi salute' - while Besiktas match is SUSPENDED due to pro-Palestine propaganda... and away fans infiltrate Sunderland

By LUKE POWER, SPORTS REPORTER and BOBBY MANZI, FOOTBALL REPORTER

Published: 16:06 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 12:19 EST, 27 November 2026

European football has endured another night of chaos with fan trouble at Marseille, Besiktas and Sunderland.

Marseille and Levski Sofia fans clashed violently at their Europa League match, with home hooligans descending on the away end with bats and metal pipes after being provoked by a Nazi salute.

Turkish side Besiktas' clash with Israeli team Hapoel Be'er Sheva was brought to a temporary halt after fans of the former unfurled a pro-Palestinian flag, leading to a clash with police.

And Sunderland's home end was infiltrated by supporters of Jagiellonia Bialystok, who had been banned for the fixture by UEFA - with some of the visitors starting brawls.

The three Europa League disturbances cast another dark shadow over football.

Marseille saw the worst events as an estimated 200-300 home hooligans entered the away end with bats, pipes, and flares.

Marseille's supporters descended on the Levski Sofia end with bats and flares

It is believed that the Marseille ultras were provoked by a Nazi salute by a Levski Sofia fan

One supporter at the Marseille-Levski Sofia match nursed a bleeding head injury

Besiktas fans unfurled a Palestine flag at their fixture against Israeli side Hapoel Be'er Sheva

They had reportedly been provoked by some of Levski's ultras, who have a long association with neo-Nazism, and Marseille's supporters responded with an antifascist chant.

In a statement released on Friday afternoon, UEFA said: 'We strongly condemn the serious incidents of violence and disorder, including the clashes involving supporters inside the stadium, that occurred in connection with the Europa League matches between Marseille and Levski Sofia as well as Besiktas and Hapoel Beer-Sheva.

'Violence, aggression, hatred and any form of provocative, discriminatory or extremist behaviour have no place in football. UEFA competitions are founded on the principles of respect, fair play, integrity and safety.

'The events witnessed at the matches run counter to these fundamental values and to UEFA’s objective, enshrined in its statutes, of ensuring that football matches are played in a spirit of peace, mutual respect and sporting fairness.

'UEFA has appointed ethics and disciplinary inspectors to conduct investigations into the incidents and examine all available evidence to establish the relevant facts and circumstances in accordance with the applicable UEFA regulatory framework.'

Some people kicked and punched each other in Marseille - another even used a fire extinguisher, according to L'Equipe.

Bulgarian news agency Bgnes, meanwhile, reported that the French hooligans also hurled bottles, flares and firecrackers.

Women and members of Levski's entourage were among the crowd, and several injured supporters had to be escorted out of the stadium, according to reports.

'Olympique de Marseille condemns the incidents that occurred on the sidelines of the match against Levski Sofia,' the hosts said in a statement.

'The swift intervention of the club's security teams restored calm, without affecting the match itself.

'The club is currently working to establish the precise circumstances of these incidents, in conjunction with the relevant authorities.'

Elsewhere, trouble spiked in the 25th minute of Besiktas' 2-1 win over Hapoel Be'er Sheva.

One fan was seen being taken away on a stretcher at the Besiktas game, which was played in Batumi, Georgia

Besiktas full-back Kassoum Ouattara hung the Palestine flag over the advertising hoarding, covering the UEFA lettering

Police had to remove some Jagiellonia Bialystok fans who had infiltrated the home end at Sunderland

The match had been moved to Batumi, Georgia due to security worries surrounding ties between Turkish and Israeli clubs. There was even tension on the pitch, as Besiktas refused to shake hands with their opponents.

After a pro-Palestine banner was revealed by Besiktas' fans, the Georgian police appeared to react with tear gas or pepper spray and batons. One fan was seen being carried away on a stretcher.

The game had to be briefly suspended, with both sets of teams and the officials going to the dressing rooms.

After the match, Besiktas full-back Kassoum Ouattara hung the Palestine flag over the UEFA lettering on the pitchside advertising hoardings.

Besiktas condemned the local police, saying they had used 'disproportionate force'.

The club also wrote: 'Upon learning that security forces were obstructing our fans' entry into the stadium, we immediately contacted the UEFA delegate, who arranged for the stadium's evacuation gates to be opened, allowing our fans to enter the stadium quickly and safely.

'We announce that steps have been taken with our Consulate General in Batumi and UEFA regarding the disproportionate force used by security forces against our fans, and state that we will closely monitor the situation until each of our fans returns safely to our country.'

Turkey and Israel have long been simmering with tension amid the conflict and numerous Turkish clubs such as Galatasaray, Fenerbahce, and Mohamed Salah's Trabzonspor came out in support of Besiktas later - despite usually being bitter rivals.

A UEFA Disciplinary ruling meant Polish club Jagiellonia Białystok weren't meant to have any away supporters at The Stadium of Light for tonight's game at Sunderland, yet plenty of them have turned up in the home end… 🫣😭pic.twitter.com/lRBvHOp16T

Jagiellonia Bialystok's supporters had been banned - but some bought tickets in the home end

Meanwhile, at the Stadium of Light, events were of a lower scale, but some away fans were seen brawling with the home faithful and police waded in to eject them.

Jagiellonia Bialystok's fans had been banned from attending the game by UEFA following disturbances between them and Levski Sofia fans earlier this month.

But around 20 of them managed to secure tickets, Sunderland believe, and squeeze into the stadium.

The club had already caught some out in advance, writing: 'The club is actively monitoring ticket purchases and has identified and cancelled tickets purchased by, or on behalf of, individuals identified as Jagiellonia supporters.

'All affected tickets will be refunded to the original purchasers.

'This restriction applies across all areas of the stadium, including home sections, and regardless of how tickets have been purchased or transferred.

'Any attempt to circumvent the restriction, including using tickets purchased through third parties or belonging to other supporters, will result in refusal of entry.

'Jagiellonia supporters without a valid entitlement to attend the fixture are strongly advised not to travel to Sunderland.

'No Jagiellonia supporters without valid permission to attend will be permitted entry into the Stadium of Light, and we strongly advise they stay away from the immediate surrounding vicinity.

'The club will continue to work closely with the relevant authorities to ensure UEFA's ruling is fully enforced and that the fixture takes place as a home supporter-only event.'

#1137. A guide to the Nature Index

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The Nature Index is a database of author affiliations and institutional relationships. The index tracks contributions to research articles published in high-quality natural-science and health-science journals, chosen based on reputation by an independent group of researchers.

The Nature Index provides absolute and fractional counts of article publication at the institutional and national level and, as such, is an indicator of global high-quality research output and collaboration. Data in the Nature Index are updated regularly, with the most recent 12 months made available under a Creative Commons licence at natureindex.com. The database is compiled by Nature Portfolio.

The Nature Index uses Count and Share to track research output. A country/territory or an institution is given a Count of 1 for each article that has at least one author from that country/territory or institution. This is the case regardless of the number of authors an article has, and it means that the same article can contribute to the Count of multiple countries/territories or institutions.

To glean a country’s, territory’s, region’s or an institution’s contribution to an article, and to ensure that they are not counted more than once, the Nature Index uses Share, a fractional count that takes into account the share of authorship on each article. The total Share available per article is 1, which is shared among all authors under the assumption that each contributed equally. For instance, an article with 10 authors means that each author receives a Share of 0.1. For authors who are affiliated with more than one institution, the author’s Share is split equally between each institution. The total Share for an institution is calculated by summing the Share for individual affiliated authors. The process is similar for countries/territories, although complicated by the fact that some institutions have overseas labs that will be counted towards host country/territory totals.

Adjusted Share accounts for the annual variation in the total number of articles in the Nature Index journals. It is arrived at by calculating the percentage difference in the total number of articles in the Index in a given year relative to the number of articles in a base year and adjusting Share values to the base year levels.

The bilateral collaboration score (CS) between two institutions A+B is the sum of each of their Shares on the papers to which both have contributed. A bilateral collaboration can be between any two institutions or countries/territories co-authoring at least one article in the journals tracked by the Nature Index.

natureindex.com users can search for specific institutions or countries and generate their own reports, ordered by Count or Share.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03474-5

Nature maintains full independence in all editorial decisions related to the content.

#1136. 37 years after fall of Berlin Wall: How divided are Germans?

Three artists share their thoughts on the reunification of East and West Germany. How do they perceive a shared "we" and what gives them cause for optimism?

When the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, ending East Germany's isolation from the West, the event was celebrated on both sides of the border. Yet, 37 years later, many people on both sides remain deeply skeptical of each other.

Surveys show that only a minority of respondents report feeling a strong sense of community between those from former East and West Germany, and many continue to perceive significant differences.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

We asked three artists from Germany with different perspectives on the history of the country's division to share their views.

Author Lea Streisand was born in 1979 and experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall firsthand while growing up in East Berlin.

In her books and essays, she has returned to her East German upbringing many times, using literature to process it.

The novel "Hufeland, at the corner of Bötzow" (2019, Ullstein), for example, recounts the period of reunification from a child's perspective.

"November 9, 1989, was simply incredible," she told DW. She was 10 years old at the time. When her mother bought her winter boots with the 100 Deutsche Marks she received from the West German state — a welcome gift given to all East German citizens — she was so disappointed that she felt like crying. But later, a friend of her parents' let her buy so many sweets at the supermarket that they lasted until Christmas.

"The disappointment really set in afterwards, with what happened over the course of the following year. It was unbelievable how quickly an entire system was suddenly swept away and a new one built up, as if to say, 'There you go. You're welcome'," Streisand recalled. "I think it was just too fast for people."

The people of East Germany, or the GDR, had brought about the fall of the Berlin Wall themselves through a civil rights movement and numerous demonstrations. For many, however, the goal was not to dissolve the state immediately but to reform it.

Among them was Anke Feuchtenberger, born in 1963 in East Berlin. Her childhood was spent in East Berlin and in the East German region of Western Pomerania, where she now lives again and feels "very much at home."

Today, she teaches at the University of Applied Sciences in Hamburg, meaning she spends time on both sides of the former divide. Feuchtenberger is often described as Germany's most influential comic artist. Her work has also garnered international acclaim.

"Back then, as artists, we tried to bring about a change through posters and flyers — to gain more freedom without immediately abolishing socialism," she explained.

At the time, the fall of the Berlin Wall stirred up mixed feelings in Feuchtenberger: "I soon realized that the creative and revolutionary aspects of our movement were very quickly being smothered by consumerism, and that nationalist tendencies — which had already been noticeable before — were coming to the fore," Feuchtenberger recalled. "That made me afraid."

Meanwhile, for photographic artist Simon Menner, born in 1978 in Emmendingen, in the West German state of Baden-Württemberg, Berlin was very far away. As Menner put it, he experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall as a child in a "rather abstract" way. Today, Berlin is his home.

In his experience, the way films and documentaries portrayed East Germany around the time of reunification was very bleak. "But West Germany in the '80s," he said, "was also bleak and very staid."

This uneven portrayal of the two parts of Germany is an issue that deeply concerns Menner — partly because he unwittingly contributed to it in a small way. Among other things, Menner's work explores the topic of surveillance and how it works.

In the archives of East Germany's Ministry for State Security, or Stasi — which are freely accessible today as part of the National Archives — he discovered a massive collection of photographs that both fascinated and horrified him and which he wanted to bring to the attention of a wider public.

His photo book "Top Secret" (2012, from publisher Hatje Cantz) features a selection of photos that offer a unique insight into the work of the Stasi. Some are eerie, while others are curious or even absurd.

Menner also tried to look into the photo archive of West Germany's Federal Intelligence Service. "I spent a year trying to gain access — without success," he said.

In hindsight, he now finds his artistic project problematic because he believes it is too one-sided, focusing exclusively on East Germany's past.

According to Menner, West Germany's intelligence services in the 1960s were not exactly models of virtue either, and he believes it is "actually high time" to critically examine this part of history as well. In his view, an honest examination of Germany's past as a whole is a prerequisite for genuine reconciliation.

Streisand believes literature can help foster mutual understanding. "Literature opens a window into experiences we haven't had ourselves," she said. "You can immerse yourself in the mind of someone who has had a different life than you have and understand what happened."

Interest in these stories remains strong. In 2023, Feuchtenberger published the nearly 500-page graphic novel "Comrade Cuckoo" (published by Reprodukt), which was the first graphic novel to be nominated for the Leipzig Book Fair Prize in the fiction category.

The story spans a childhood in the fictional East German village of Pritschitanow in the 1960s in the GDR to the post-Reunification era. In it, Feuchtenberger weaves autobiographical memories of her upbringing with fantastical and fictional elements.

The artist said she was surprised "that, so long after the fall of the wall, my stories have sparked such great interest in the West."

In particular, the fact that the main character, Kerstin, rarely sees her parents because they both work full-time is a topic that often comes up at readings. In the GDR, everyone had the right to work, she said. At the same time, it was a civic duty.

Could the West German interest in this stem from the fact that full-time employment for both parents has long been less common in the West? It's possible, said Feuchtenberger.

When looking toward their shared future, the two East German women are more optimistic than Menner, from West Germany.

"In Berlin, I often don't even notice anymore whether I'm in the West or the East," said Menner. "But when it comes to sociopolitical issues, politicians should listen to older and younger people more closely," he added, referring to the recent election successes of far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD . "Otherwise, things are going to get difficult in the near future."

"It's very important to step outside our own bubble because people all over the world are facing problems. Constantly focusing on this German-German divide that has emerged between the groups doesn't help," said Feuchtenberger.

"For me personally, the whole issue of borders has somehow dissolved," she explained. This is due in no small part to the many trips abroad that have taken her to various places around the world.

Moreover, in her hometown near the Polish border, she observes how animals couldn't care less about the border. "They come from the east and the west and do whatever they want," she said. That's why she also gave "Comrade Cuckoo" the working title "A German Animal in a German Forest," "because I found the absurdity of an animal having a nationality so funny."

"This East-West thing — our children won't have any interest in it at all," said Streisand. "Young people don't care where their parents come from. Can I get a job that will support a family? Do I have to go to war? Right now, completely different things are relevant."

This article was originally written in German.

#1135. Man Utd show fight on night of chaos to give Carrick a glimpse of hope

So maybe there is some fight left in the old dog yet?

At half-time, Manchester United looked down and out and Michael Carrick’s reign as manager as good as finished.

Roma were 2-0 in front and coasting, gorging on a desperate United’s litany of errors, and there was full-scale mutiny in the stands at Old Trafford. A fifth defeat in six matches and the club’s longest winless run for 48 years beckoned. It was toxic on and off the pitch.

And then something changed. United, from being a dishevelled, disorganised mess, suddenly seemed to remember who they were supposed to be and what they were supposed to represent. Surrender gave way to fight. A team that had been feeling sorry for themselves discovered some pride. A crowd that had been baying for blood turned Old Trafford into a bear pit of a very different kind, and Roma simply did not know what had hit them.

This club have served up some famous comebacks over the decades, but it was hard to think of too many occasions when the mood and momentum had shifted this violently from one half to the next.

United fans were in open revolt in that first half, releasing green and gold balloons in protests before kick-off and then throwing tennis balls on to the pitch amid furious chanting against the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe. The players looked like they would rather have been anywhere else.

And yet by the 86th minute Matheus Cunha’s wild celebrations were encapsulating a wild night, the Brazilian ripping off his shirt after his dramatic winner before launching himself into a delirious crowd drunk on the euphoria of a victory that had seemed improbable in the extreme at the interval, when boos cascaded from the stands.

Whether this proves little more than a thrilling, heroic interlude in the endgame for Carrick, or the start of a genuine turnaround, is hard to know. And, let’s be clear, there was so much about the first-half performance to concern the hierarchy, who came under persistent, furious attack from fans at war with an ownership it reviles and wants gone.

But the second half stood firmly at odds with the shambolic display that had preceded it and suggested all may not be quite lost just yet.

Aston Villa visit Old Trafford on Sunday in the final game before the international break and, if Carrick can follow this with another win, then it will be intriguing to see where the Old Trafford board goes from there.

Carrick may at least have been encouraged by some of the things Bruno Fernandes said after the game, not least that he warranted being dropped against Bournemouth. And it was the captain who kick-started the fightback against Roma, albeit at the second attempt.

He had won the penalty after being fouled by Gianluca Mancini only to then contrive to miss it. But a retake was ordered for encroachment and, given a second bite at the cherry, Fernandes made no mistake.

Eight games for Bruno Fernandes without a goal or assist but he has finally broken that drought.

United showing a bit more fight and trying to put pressure on the third-choice keeper as he plays the ball out.

No shots or shots on target for United. One shot on target for Roma and one goal.

But Bruno Fernandes picks the ball up on the right wing from Diallo and fizzes a low ball across the face of goal. Mbeumo can’t quite connect and it is swept away from the feet of Cunha at the far post before he can tap it in.

This is obviously the last thing United would have wanted. The crowd – previously cheering every ball forward and every challenge – have gone quite quiet.

But just like that, Roma get the breakthrough.

United lose the ball and are carved open. Mora sends a long ball across the field and finds Soulé completely unmarked on the edge of the box. He brings it down, makes a short run and slots it past Lammens low at the near post.

Mainoo sends a nice pass out to Diallo on the right who sends a ball to Bruno Fernandes on the overlap. His ball into the box is quickly blocked but Mainoo has started very brightly and draws a foul in the next passage of play.

Yoro wins the ball in midfield and United get a bit of possession up the field but a sloppy pass from Dalot gifts it back to Roma and now the visitors are probing the United final third.

As the Champions League anthems plays, fans have released their yellow and green balloons from the stands in protest against the club’s owners.

A mix of boos and cheers from around the ground.

He’s already scored three in the Champions League, and could be looking eagerly at United’s shaky mentality to add to those numbers. He is the top scorer in Europe’s top five leagues in this calendar year, beating the likes of Lamine Yamal and Harry Kane.

Gasperini’s man-to-man style emphasises his skill in one-on-one situations, where his pace and drive with the ball make him a handful for even the best defenders.

Galatasaray are already 2-0 up on Stuttgart, while Sporting have found the breakthrough against Shakhtar Donetsk in the early kick-offs.

Manchester United fans are planning a series of in-stadium demonstrations at Old Trafford tonight in protest at the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s ownership.

Thousands of green and gold balloons – a nod to the club’s original colours as Newton Heath – are set to be released from the Stretford End when the Champions League music plays out ahead of kick-off.

There had been plans to bring a banner into the stadium bearing the words: “No new stadium, we want new owners” but that was blocked, apparently on the grounds of Uefa’s inability to sanction it in time.

The Glazers and Ratcliffe have come under growing attack this season with the club’s regular match going supporters at war with the owners.

A separate fans’ group has also been encouraging fans to join in anti Glazers and Ratcliffe chants in the 21st minute or, more specifically, after 20 minutes and 5 seconds: 20.05 is a nod to 2005, the year the Glazers completed their hostile takeover at Old Trafford.

The main surprise for Roma is in goal, as with first-choice keeper Svilar out already, it has been confirmed that backup keeper Pierluigi Gollini has injured his back today. He has been replaced by Colombian Devis Vásquez in goal.

Roma: Vásquez; Balerdi, Mancini, Hermoso; Rensch, de Roon, Mora, Wesley; Soulé, Cristante; Malen

We have confirmation, Martínez is on the bench. He is replaced by Ayden Heaven while Bruno Fernandes is still with the captain’s armband in midfield. Kobbie Mainoo gets the nod as he returns from injury, along with Mateus Cunha and Mason Mount.

Your United team for tonight's #UCL clash 👊 https://t.co/TD9F6RjeAB

Lisandro Martínez has been dropped by Michael Carrick in the wake of his red card madness against Chelsea.

The United manager has opted to pair Ayden Heaven in central defence with Harry Maguire for the Roma game with Martinez dropping to the bench.

The Argentina defender received a second yellow card for planting an elbow in Wesley Fofana’s face in Saturday’s 2-0 defeat at Chelsea when he was also culpable for the first goal.

Martinez has been in dire form this season and was fined and publicly apologised after publicly criticising director of football Jason Wilcox and the Old Trafford board in the wake of the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid.

Kobbie Mainoo returns to midfield after missing the last four games through injury.

Ayden Heaven has just come out to speak with Prime Video, which has led Gabby Logan to assume that means that Lisandro Martínez will not start for Michael Carrick tonight.

Speaking with her, former United legend Wayne Rooney has said the Argentine has “simply not been good enough” and should not necessarily feature again under Carrick.

When Alan Shearer was asked if he would include Martínez on a team sheet tonight, he did not mince his words, calling him a “liability”.

Ahead of the confirmed line-ups coming out shortly, there are certain players we know we will not be seeing today.

Patrick Dorgu (hamstring), Luke Shaw (unspecified) and Benjamin Sesko (shin) remain sidelined for United, while Marcus Rashford and Amad Diallo will be assessed before the match.

There are no new concerns for Gasperini after his side’s latest match, the 5-2 win over Udinese, but he remains unable to select Muhammed Bah (ACL), Paulo Dybala, Manu Kone (thigh), Lorenzo Pellegrini (thigh) and first-choice keeper Mile Svilar (stress fracture, foot).

Happy Tuesday and thanks for tuning in to tonight’s coverage of Manchester United against Roma.

It’s matchday four of the Champions League and Michael Carrick’s side host their Serie A opponents having failed to win any of their last nine matches across all competitions. Since their win against Sabah back in September (must feel like years ago to Carrick), they have suffered chastening defeats in Europe to Atlético Madrid and then Cesc Fabregas’s Como. This has been coupled with dismal performances in the Premier League, most recently a 2-0 defeat at the hands of Chelsea, where Lisandro Martínez was sent off for two ridiculous fouls.

Lisandro Martinez is shown a second yellow card following a VAR review 🟥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max ➡️https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/VLcAMNdqgZ

All in all, there is the feeling that Carrick is simply a dead man walking, limping towards the international break after the United hierarchy decided on a stay of execution in their crisis talks earlier this month. If the beleaguered manager has any hope at all of hanging on to his job, he needs convincing results tonight and against Aston Villa on the weekend.

Despite the doom-mongering that circles the club, Carrick maintains that he has buried the hatchet with Bruno Fernandes following his captain’s public criticisms of the club, insisting that “the dressing room is a good place” in his pre-match press conference (more on that to come).

The visitors on the other hand, managed by Gian Piero Gasperini – who replaced Claudio Ranieri last summer – are certainly having a better time of it. They got off to a slow start in Europe, drawing with Fernebahce in their opening match but coming agonisingly close to stunning Real Madrid on matchday two at home. They went 3-1 up before three late goals snatched victory for Madrid.

They bounced back with a convincing 4-0 win over Slovan Bratislava and their domestic campaign is off to an incredibly promising start. They are currently unbeaten in Serie A with seven wins and three draws. They sit third and are the highest scoring side, with 28 goals from their 10 games. Free-flowing though their attack is, there a certainly defensive frailties there to exploit as they conceded three in a six-goal thriller against Napoli, as well as two in both matches against Cagliari and Udinese.

It has been 19 years since Carrick was part of a United side that thrashed Roma 7-1 at Old Trafford, with the midfielder scoring two. Tonight he faces that same opponent with his job hanging by a thread and it remains to be seen if his team can produce any semblance of that spark to turn the tide. Feel free to drop us your score predictions in the comments – bragging rights on the line for the winner.

We’ll be bringing you team news, previews from the managers and more ahead of kick-off at 8pm!
