#1070. What to watch in UEFA Champions League: Manchester United face defensive crisis in tough visit to Sporting

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Another week of Champions League football comes to a close on Wednesday night as plenty of teams on the top-eight or even top-24 bubble find themselves with work to do. A shock loss to Club Brugge means that there is pressure on Inter as they face Stuttgart at the San Siro; certainly, if they are to take up a top-eight berth, this is a game they are going to have to win.

Do Manchester United have such lofty aspirations? It is with the Red Devils we start, and no wonder, given their trying run of form lately. That they do have as many wins as defeats from their first four games is almost a surprise, but a difficult fixture list shows no sign of easing for Mauricio Pochettino as his side faces Sporting in Lisbon tonight.

If there was a silver lining to the very dark clouds over Manchester United on Sunday, it would have been that there is at least plenty of time to cure what ails them in the Premier League. A point from safety is a disastrous place for such an august team to be at any point in the domestic season, but when there is more than 70% of it left to play, at least the danger is not yet cataclysmic. As for the Champions League, well, United are drifting nearer to that point.

With half their games played, they have six points. Not bad, you would have to say, good enough for 17th place in the league phase. The trouble is that their remaining four games all look difficult indeed: RB Leipzig and Bayern Munich at Old Trafford either side of Christmas, then a trip to a Villarreal outfit that should have plenty to play for on the final day. Tonight's visit to Sporting might be as good a shot at three points as Pochettino gets, and the Portuguese giants have three wins from four. He will not want to be trying to accrue four-plus points in three games.

It's all feeling very high stakes in league and Europe, the sort of moment when clear heads are needed. Not one for doom and gloom, or for Kobbie Mainoo to tell United's in-house channel "we're at the lowest we've ever been and no one's coming to save us." Then again, he's not wrong.

Already this club looks like it's doom-spiraling. It's on Pochettino to fix that. His first task will surely be to rustle up a defensive quartet who at least don't magnify each other's flaws. Does Matthijs de Ligt need time out to find the sharpness he so lacked against Liverpool? Can anyone fill in at left back? Diogo Dalot, still, really? Their organization will be tested against a Sporting side that attacks quickly and centrally, qualities that should terrify a backline that will likely be shielded by the slow-moving Mainoo and Youri Tielemans.

Sporting always score, their 22-game streak of goals in the group stage and league phase a record for a Portuguese club. Right now it looks like United are doomed to forever concede. This could get dicey.

In spite of what you might assume about Italian clubs, Inter's success at home and on the continent has not always been underlaid with defensive excellence. Certainly, there have been some memorable individual displays, none more so than Yann Sommer standing tall against the Barcelona onslaught, but great defense tends not to be about one player doing the spectacular over and over. After all, sometimes excellence is required because of mistakes elsewhere.

And right now mistakes are plaguing Inter across the field. Their 12 Serie A games have seen the concession of 17 goals, two in the final 10 minutes at Atalanta turning what might have been a valuable 4-2 win on the road into a chastening draw. It's the same story in the Champions League, where there have been a competition-high four errors leading to goals and another three leading to shots. Those sorts of numbers may not be very predictive, but in this case they feel indicative of a defense that has taken a step down from a level that wasn't that high to begin with.

Some of that problem lies with recruitment. It might have been time to move on from Sommer, but Josep Martinez has not proven himself to have been the ready-made replacement in the wings he might have been. Francesco Acerbi and Stefan de Vrij were similarly long in the tooth, and there was an argument for swapping out experience for experience in the form of ex-Manchester City duo Manuel Akanji and John Stones. The issue when you keep going for old guys, though, is that some of them are on the downslope (Akanji) and others can't stay fit (Stones). Being a bit too old might be an issue in midfield too.

These failings are being particularly exposed in the Champions League, where Club Brugge, Real Madrid and even Shakhtar Donetsk have ended up with good shot volume and expected goals. Domestically, Inter allow a solid 1.1 non-penalty expected goals (npxG) per game, but maybe that says more about the field in Serie A. Or maybe there's just a lot of air in four Champions League games in which 7.6 npxG has been allowed.

It might be true that, as the graphic indicates, Inter's defense has stabilized a bit of late after a bad start to the season, although it probably did not feel like that when Milan were scoring three goals off 0.62 xG. It also helps no end when the attack is firing, Francesco Pio Esposito giving Cristian Chivu every manager's favorite sort of headache. However, against a Stuttgart side that can test the best defenses -- 1.96 npxG per Bundesliga game, 2.09 in the Champions League -- that defense is going to have to get its house in order.

Has it finally clicked for Florian Wirtz? Well, maybe. The 23-year-old leads the Premier League in chances created, trails only Declan Rice for assists provided, and is one of only five players with over two expected assists from open play this season. All that, and he ranks in the top 20 for shots and in the 91st percentile for npxG. At 11 games, it might be worth considering a few caveats. Nineteen of his 33 chances created came against Brentford and Manchester United. In the match against the former, there were an awful lot of sideways passes that resulted in long-range shots from the receiver, a chance created in law if not in spirit. As for the other game, well, it was against Manchester United. Ten-man Manchester United at that.

Wirtz can still get locked out of high-leverage games against Arsenal and Manchester City. The Wirtz who, in Bayer Leverkusen colors, seemed the surest nine-figure bet in the game tended to excel whatever the opposition. For Liverpool, it has to be just right. A game that is more up and down with fewer demands on him to break down a low block. Opponents who are slightly less muscular than the Premier League average (see Manchester United). There is still a suspicion that a league as physical and fast as England's might lessen Wirtz's effectiveness, though the man himself would contend otherwise. He says he is getting used to the demands of the league.

"I can't really say that I've changed that much," he said when asked how he had adapted to life with Liverpool. "I've become a bit better on a physical level and that's the only reason that could explain it."

Credit also went to Andoni Iraola, who has afforded Wirtz a largely settled run as the primary creator in a 4-2-3-1. "He is bringing me back in a place where I was maybe two years ago where I played really good football," the German international said. "I can feel that he gives me the confidence and I'm really happy about that. I'm just trying to give him back what he gives me."

Expect this good form to continue in Europe, where Wirtz has generally looked a more threatening player than he does in the Premier League. In part that's a function of the aforementioned physicality. It's probably also true that the likes of LASK, Villarreal, Qarabag and Wednesday's opponents Club Brugge would not exactly be pulling up trees in the Premier League either. A chance, then, for Wirtz to build even more momentum.

#1068. Depleted PSG attack shows vulnerability in 2-2 Champions League draw with Roma

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Have Paris Saint-Germain been defanged? It is too soon to say if injuries have laid low the Champions League's biggest beast, but on the evidence of Wednesday's 2-2 draw with Roma, there might not be quite the same fear factor when opponents find themselves face to face with the kings of Europe's jungle.

Without Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and Desire Doue, both of whom are expected to miss most, if not all, of this season with knee injuries, there simply was not the final-third threat in PSG's ranks to keep Roma honest without the ball. That was all the more pronounced given that Ousmane Dembele was left on the bench until the penalty with which PSG took a 2-1 lead. Maghnes Akliouche, Senny Mayulu and Ferran Torres are talented forwards, the last good enough to win a World Cup final for Spain. Pair one or even two of them with the potential Ballon d'Or winners who started for PSG in the Champions League final, and the drop-off is not particularly significant.

Of course, it might be that Luis Enrique is not particularly minded to see how good his reserves could be flanking Dembele. It would make sense. The Frenchman's fitness needs careful managing at the best of times. With PSG having won their first four league-phase games, there was no pressing need to load up minutes on a player who will surely be needed in the spring. It was a similar story at the base of PSG's team, Ilia Zabarnyi preferred to Marquinhos, another who does well to hit a dozen games before Christmas. This might be a vision of the months ahead for an injury-addled PSG, but it might just be a team that has never taken the league phase particularly seriously not taking the league phase particularly seriously.

Whatever the longer-term view, on the field this evening, PSG's attack lacked the bite to keep Roma backing off. There is a good chance that any team managed by Gian Piero Gasperini might just go man-to-man whoever the opposition, but the fearlessness with which the Giallorossi hurtled around the Parc des Princes was a sure sign they weren't checking over their shoulder quite as much.

Instead, they felt empowered to push on, center back Mario Hermoso on hand to roll in the opener inside the box after an excellent run by Matias Soule. Again, the caveat to assessing how future opponents might take on PSG is that Hermoso has been box-crashing from defense all through this season. You can't be sure he wouldn't have been in the same spot even if he were marking Doue or Kvaratskhelia.

What you can know is that Roma's aggression when PSG had the ball in open play was not what cost them. Nuno Mendes' ability to blow by his man created issues, and Achraf Hakimi got his usual shots and shot assists from advanced positions. They could have beaten Roma, but aside from the fullbacks and a few darts into the area by Joao Neves, there was not much to scare Mile Svilar in the champions' lineup.

Instead, it was familiar failings that cost Roma, who might be a real dark horse for this competition when they can successfully defend a corner. Zabarnyi did not even have to win a duel to turn Mayulu's delivery home, just standing in the space between two white shirts at the near post. PSG's second, from the penalty spot, was a Roma confection too. Wesley could argue that Svilar should have been off his line quicker when Hakimi charged in behind, but did the Brazilian need to put his arms on his man at the exact moment he broke into the box? Wesley was lucky not to get a straight red.

In such favorable positions, prime PSG often blitz their opponents. This time, even with Dembele on the field, they could not get clear. Gasperini had an ace of his own on the bench, Donyell Malen sparking Roma after his introduction. A driving run and cutback from the left had PSG scrambling, Vitinha's arm blocking a shot to hand the visitors a penalty that Malen converted.

Had a third goal come, it would probably have been for Roma, Hermoso blazing over late on. There was something more in this for Roma, who remain outside the top 24 despite such impressive displays against Real Madrid, Manchester United and now the holders. As for PSG, there will be time for Luis Enrique to work out how his side dominates Europe with its attack so limited. It would appear there is work to do.

#1065. Intelligent women get less help at work, study finds

Women who scored high on intelligence tests were seen as more hostile by their teammates and got less help, a new study finds. High-scoring men faced no such penalty. Research explains why.

High intelligence is usually counted as an asset at work. But a new study suggests that for women, it can also lead to worse treatment from colleagues.

Across 826 people in the United States and China, women who scored higher on an intelligence test were rated by their teammates as more hostile, received less help and were undermined more often. Men with high scores did not receive such treatment, and in one group, they were treated better.

The study examined whether people's cognitive ability affects how their teammates treat them and whether that differs between women and men.

Since it was published this year, Nitya Chawla, an associate professor at UCL School of Management in London and the researcher behind the study, says women have written to her saying the findings matched their own experience at work. Some told her they had wondered whether they were to blame for hostility.

The researchers ran two studies. The first followed 432 business students at a US public university working in small teams on a consulting project for real organizations. The second surveyed 394 full-time employees working in teams at a financial company in China.

Intelligence here means cognitive ability measured with a standardized test of reasoning and problem-solving that employers use in hiring. Teammates were not told of anyone's scores. They rated one another, and a few weeks later each person reported how much help they had received and how often they had been undermined, for instance by having information withheld.

The effects were small, and the study shows a link, not proof that colleagues' perceptions caused the treatment. Participants reported help and mistreatment themselves, and the study did not look at race or ethnicity.

In the student group, the difference between women and men was no longer statistically significant when two participants with extremely low scores were included.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The researchers point to social role theory, the idea that people expect men and women to fit traditional roles: men as capable and assertive, women as warm and supportive. A woman with high cognitive ability breaks that expectation, and colleagues may assume she lacks warmth.

"It's that automatic, implicit assumption that takes place alongside the presence of intelligence that then drives these more negative interpersonal behaviors," Chawla told DW.

In both groups, women with higher scores were rated as more hostile. Among the employees in China, they were also rated as less warm. Women seen as more hostile reported less help, both with their work and on a personal level, and more undermining.

The team also checked whether the women were simply behaving differently. Higher-scoring women were rated as somewhat more domineering, but that did not explain why they received less help or more mistreatment. The findings point to colleagues' assumptions, Chawla says, rather than to anything the women did.

No, men with high intelligence scores do not face the same treatment. Among the students in the United States, a man's score made no difference to how his teammates rated or treated him.

Among the employees in China, men with higher scores were rated as less hostile, received more help and were mistreated less often. The authors suggest the difference between the two groups may reflect cultural differences in gender norms, but they did not test this.

No, Chawla says. "That would be really the wrong conclusion to draw."

Small effects still matter, she argues, because they are experienced day after day. Over time, this kind of treatment can lead to anxiety, self-doubt and a sense of not belonging. "These experiences and these feelings can become very, very burdensome over time," she said.

Chawla puts the responsibility on workplaces rather than on women. Managers, she says, should track how team members treat one another, and organizations should hold regular check-ins to see whether employees are getting equal support.

Individuals can ask themselves a simple question, she says: would they react the same way if that colleague were a man?

This article is an excerpt from our podcast Science Unscripted.

#1064. 2026 Concacaf W Championship: What to know, how to watch as USWNT aim to punch ticket to World Cup

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Just when you think you're going to settle in for a long winter's nap, there's more high-stakes women's soccer to watch. The 2026 Concacaf W Championship paves the way to the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup in Brazil and the 2028 Summer Olympics, and eight national teams from the region will play a knockout bracket starting Friday, Nov. 27.

With World Cup and Olympic berths decided along the way, fans can watch all of the 2026 Concacaf W Championship on CBS Sports Golazo Network and Paramount+.

Here's everything you need to know about the upcoming tournament:

All times Eastern -- all games will air on Paramount+

Saturday, Dec. 5 (third-place match and final)

The Concacaf W Championship is a senior women's national team championship tournament that doubles as the region's qualifier for both the World Cup and the Olympics.

This year's edition has a new format that sends teams to the 2027 World Cup and 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. The biggest change is the quarterfinal bracket. The top two ranked teams, the United States and Canada, earned byes into the tournament. Jamaica, Costa Rica, Mexico, Panama, Haiti, and El Salvador all earned spots through the Concacaf W Qualifiers.

Back in 2022, eight finalists were placed into two groups of four, with the top two teams in each advancing into the semifinals and clinching World Cup spots. Third-place teams were given a chance to qualify in the inter-confederation playoffs. 2022 was also the first year the competition served as both a World Cup and Olympic qualifier, but only the champion and the winner of a two-leg playoff clinched Olympic berths.

This year, the group stages are gone, and a single quarterfinal will decide who qualifies directly. In 2026, the quarterfinal winners all earn a place in the 2027 World Cup, and quarterfinal losers compete in a play-in round, with the two winners earning spots in the inter-confederation playoffs in February 2027.

The two Concacaf W Championship finalists and the third-place finisher qualify for the 2028 Summer Games. The United States are hosts of the 2028 Olympics and qualify automatically, so if they finish in the top three, the fourth-place team takes the remaining Olympic spot.

The U.S. women's national team will face El Salvador for the first time in program history. El Salvador are the USWNT's first new opponent since playing Zambia in the Olympic group stage in July 2024.

The USWNT step into the competition as reigning Concacaf W Championship winners. They've won the last three tournaments and hold a record nine all-time titles. The USWNT won all five of their games in the 2022 W Championship without conceding a goal and outscored opponents 13-0. The USWNT are 106W-1D-0L in matches against teams ranked outside of FIFA's Top 25, drawing only to Costa Rica 0-0 in July 2024 in Washington, D.C.

Manager Emma Hayes named a 23-player roster for the tournament, but recently made some changes following the 2026 NWSL Championship. Trinity Rodman, who sustained a shoulder injury, has been replaced by Jaedyn Shaw, and Shaw will be replaced by Lia Godfrey on the U-23 roster.

Kansas City Current defender Laney Rouse was also ruled out of the U-23 roster and is replaced by Denver Summit FC defender Natalie Means.

El Salvador have never qualified for a Women's World Cup and will make their debut at the Concacaf W Championship. They qualified for the tournament by winning Group F with three clean sheets against Honduras, Barbados, and Trinidad & Tobago.

Head coach Eric Acuna is still leading the group after previous investigations into alleged abusive conduct,  and he publicly criticized players just last month after losses to Paraguay.

Players are trying to move forward and are led by Brenda Ceren, who led the team with five goals, followed by Danielle Fuentes with four, during the Concacaf W Qualifiers.

#1063. How Emile Heskey fell into a sketchy world peddling controversial drugs: From England star worth £12m to bankruptcy, unpaid tax and a bitter divorce

Published: 07:00 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 07:35 EST, 26 November 2026

Emile Heskey is standing in a warehouse, dressed in a black adidas tracksuit, trying to sell you a jar of curious sweet treats.

He smiles into the camera with the gentle-giant warmth that characterised his football career – but Heskey is in unfamiliar territory.

Behind him, stacked on shelf after shelf, are containers full of Supreme CBD gummies.

The man who scored in England's 5-1 thrashing of Germany in 2001, who scored 110 Premier League goals for Leicester, Liverpool, Birmingham, Wigan and Aston Villa plus seven more for his country, is, remarkably, trying to flog you an assortment of products containing cannabidiol, a legal but controversial ingredient derived from cannabis.

Today, he is promoting a tub of CBD strawberry gummies, as well as oil. If you fancy an exclusive discount, there's a special code bearing his name.

‘I swear by these products for my sleep,’ he writes in the caption on Instagram. ‘They have been fantastic for me for years now!’

Emile Heskey spends his days trying to flog controversial Supreme CBD products (Instagram: theemileheskey)

He is one of multiple former footballers promoting the products for ex-Olympic boxer Anthony Fowler - despite their illegal claims about the supposed health benefits

Heskey, 48, was once one of English football's most respected players. He won 62 caps for England, appearing at two World Cups. He won five trophies at Liverpool and two League Cups at Leicester.

Occasionally mocked for his lack of goals – he averaged roughly one every five games during his club career – he carried himself with humour and grace. Since retiring, his reputation has helped him secure roles with England's youth pathway and Leicester's women's team, as well as occasional punditry work for the BBC.

In September, he scored in an England legends match against Poland, playing alongside John Terry and Robbie Fowler. This month, he was a guest of honour at Liverpool's Anfield VIP Experience. He remains a regular on the speakers' circuit, with more appearances booked before Christmas.

All of which begs the question: what is he doing promoting Supreme CBD? Why is he filming several videos a month for a company with such a troubled regulatory record?

Where once he shared a dressing room with Steven Gerrard and David Beckham, he now shares an ambassadorial roster with Katie Price.

It is unclear whether Heskey is aware of the concerns surrounding Supreme CBD products, or the repeated occasions on which the company has fallen foul of advertising rules.

Its founder, Anthony Fowler, a former Team GB Olympic boxer, has made unsubstantiated claims that his cannabidiol products can help treat mental health conditions and autism in children.

There is likely a financial incentive for Heskey, although the terms of any arrangement are unclear. Equally, he appears genuinely convinced of the products' benefits. He claims the oil has done wonders for his sleep and eased his aches and pains.

Heskey's wife Chantelle has issued divorce proceedings - and claims he cancelled a holiday with their kids to go away with his new partner instead

Heskey and his new partner Jade Slusarczyk spent two weeks together in Cyprus and Greece

Chantelle branded Heskey 'vile' and claimed he deleted her comment on an Instagram post about the new couple's holiday

That may well be true. The NHS acknowledges that CBD has some medical uses, but warns that the ‘quality and content’ of products sold online can be uncertain and that they ‘may be illegal and potentially dangerous’. Nor is there any guarantee that products sold in health stores will be of ‘good quality’.

Supreme CBD have repeatedly breached advertising rules. In June, the Advertising Standards Authority took action over the company's continued use of prohibited claims that CBD could treat, prevent or cure human disease.

The regulator has also upheld complaints about celebrity promotions that failed to make clear they were advertisements.

Supreme CBD have made claims that their products can treat anxiety, insomnia and depression. Such medicinal claims are prohibited in advertising for products that have not been authorised as medicines. It is uncomfortable ground for Heskey to find himself on.

Last year, Fowler also spoke about refusing chemotherapy for his two-year-old daughter's tumour, claiming CBD oil had had a 'massive' effect on it instead. Price, a paid brand ambassador, amplified those claims on her own social media channels, including posted to her 1.6million followers on X that the tumour had 'shrunk' as a result.

British medical and food safety authorities advise that CBD should not be given to those under the age of 18.

CBD can also affect how other medicines work, meaning anyone using it alongside other treatments should seek medical advice. Certain medicinal CBD treatments require regular monitoring because of their potential effects on the liver.

It is not unusual for former sportspeople to struggle with insomnia, depression or persistent pain after retirement. In a digital world where anyone can extol the virtues of a product to thousands of followers, it is perhaps unsurprising that cannabis oil has attracted so much attention. Some users say it has helped them.

Heskey celebrates with David Beckham after scoring for England against Denmark at the 2002 World Cup

Many of Heskey's almost 100,000 Instagram followers appear equally enthusiastic, with comments beneath his posts endorsing the benefits he describes.

And Heskey is hardly alone among former footballers. Supreme CBD products have also been endorsed by former Arsenal and England playmaker Paul Merson – who has his name on a bundle of his 'favourite' products available to buy on the company's website – Heskey's old Liverpool team-mate Chris Kirkland, Southampton hero Matt Le Tissier and ex-Nottingham Forest goalkeeper Mark Crossley, while ex-Liverpool striker John Aldridge has insisted the product was ‘good for me’.

Life after football has, at times, been rather messy for Heskey.

In 2009, his wealth was estimated at £12million. He had built a clean-cut image and maintained a relatively low profile away from the pitch. Yet just a year later, in 2010, he was declared bankrupt.

His subsequent business dealings have brought further difficulties. Earlier this year, Heskey became caught up in a legal dispute surrounding an allegedly fraudulent £15m takeover of Cypriot club Apollon Limassol by British businessman Craig Gabriel.

Heskey had been lined up to become the face of the takeover and a club director. There is no suggestion of wrongdoing on his part.

In 2023, Heskey was found to have defaulted on £92,000 in tax relating to his work as a football development officer between 2017 and 2020. He was handed a £42,000 penalty.

That same year, a celebrity bar and restaurant he had funded, and which was overseen by his wife Chantelle, was wound up by the courts with debts totalling £163,000.

Former England footballer Heskey has found love with former Miss Blackpool Slusarczyk

Parea, which opened in 2018, had been a regular haunt of footballers and television personalities, including members of the Real Housewives of Cheshire cast. But a local catering company applied to have the business wound up over unpaid debts.

The restaurant had previously made headlines in 2019 when its first anniversary party featured sushi served on a semi-naked woman lying on a table, her modesty largely preserved by strategically placed leaves and pieces of salmon.

In 2024, Heskey faced further financial difficulties linked to his involvement in a celebrity investment scheme that became embroiled in a £1.6billion tax dispute.

The scheme was reportedly operated by Ingenious Media, a financing company that backed dozens of films. Investors were said to include Beckham, Gerrard, Jeremy Paxman, Robbie Williams and Heskey, with a minimum investment of £50,000.

Gerrard and the composer Andrew Lloyd Webber were among those who launched legal proceedings against HSBC in 2018, alleging that the bank had ‘dishonestly assisted’ Ingenious Media.

In the same year, Heskey was ordered to pay almost £200,000 in a dispute involving an unpaid £1.63m tax bill.

His personal life has also become complicated. Heskey appears to be estranged from his wife Chantelle, whom he married in 2014 and with whom he has four children. In August, she branded him ‘vile’ following a holiday he took with his new partner.

Heskey had gone public with his relationship with Jade Slusarczyk, a former Sky Sports walk-on girl accompanying darts players to the oche, in July. Within a month, the couple were holidaying in Cyprus and Greece, sharing photographs of their trip on Instagram.

Parea, a popular Cheshire bar loved by footballers and celebrities and owned by Heskey and his wife, was wound up with debts of £163,000

‘The best two weeks away with you,’ he wrote. The posts provoked an angry response from Chantelle, who has begun divorce proceedings and accused Heskey of letting his family down in comments beneath the photographs. She subsequently claimed that Heskey had deleted her comment and described him as ‘vile’.

Daily Mail Sport has contacted Mrs Heskey's representatives on multiple occasions, but they have declined to comment.

Emile and Chantelle have two sons, Reigan and Jaden, both footballers, and two younger daughters, Milanna and Mendez. Jaden made his Manchester City debut in the Carabao Cup last season and is now on loan at Sheffield Wednesday, while Reigan was sold to Cologne in the summer.

Speaking to Daily Mail Sport last year, Heskey praised his sons' athletic ability and suggested that both could one day play for England's senior team. He was happy to talk on that occasion, speaking as he helped coach children at a football camp.

This time, however, Daily Mail Sport has been met with silence. We have made repeated attempts, through multiple reporters, to put questions to Heskey about his involvement with Supreme CBD. His representatives have either declined to comment or failed to respond.

We wanted to know whether he was aware of the advertising rulings against Supreme CBD, and whether he had any concerns about the medical claims made by its founder. We would also have welcomed his account of the personal and financial difficulties described here.

And so we are left watching Heskey from afar, returning to the warehouse for video after video, smiling and cracking jokes with Fowler.

Heskey scores the fifth goal in England's 5-1 trouncing of Germany in 2001

We have made repeated attempts to put questions to Heskey about his involvement with Supreme CBD. His representatives have either declined to comment or failed to respond

‘When you find the best dose for you, there's no going back,’ he declares in the caption to one post from October.

Perched on a green sofa, encouraging his followers to buy products from a company with a deeply controversial advertising record, he seems entirely at ease.

Whether Heskey has any reservations about the business whose products he so enthusiastically promotes is something we would dearly like to know.

For now, the former England striker is still smiling for the camera.

#1061. What are fossil fuels?

They are in our shampoo bottles, power our cars and heat our homes. But what actually are fossil fuels, and why do they matter?

Whether in the form of crumbly rock, odorless gas or slick black liquid, ancient organic compounds have powered the flourishing of modern life. But now they threaten to make the planet unlivable for many plants, animals and humans.

The collective term refers to coal, oil and natural gas — a group of energy sources that contain carbon and hydrogen.

They started life hundreds of millions of years ago as living plants and animals. When they died, they sank to the bottom of oceans and swamps where they decomposed under layers of sediment.

Over time, this matter was buried deeper and deeper into the earth, subjecting it to increasing pressure and heat which changed its chemical composition. Plants and trees transformed into coal, whereas microscopic plankton and algae became oil and — if the heat and pressure increased further — gas.

Today fossil fuels can be found in the earth's crust all around the world although some countries, such as the US, Saudi Arabia and Russia, have bigger reserves than others.

Coal, found in underground coal beds, is extracted by mining, whereas oil and gas, found in reservoirs beneath the land and ocean, are accessed by drilling.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Since the early 19th Century, when the discovery and exploitation of fossil fuel reserves powered the Industrial Revolution, our use of them has skyrocketed, increasing eight-fold since 1950.

Today they provide 80% of our energy needs through heating, electricity generation and transport.

We transform them into energy either by burning them directly in furnaces that warm up our homes and businesses, or in power plants to heat water into steam which then generates electricity. When it comes to transport, crude oil is refined into a range of products such as diesel, gasoline and kerosene that are burned in the engines of automobiles, airplanes and ships. Natural gas is also sometimes compressed for use in cars and buses.

But fossil fuels are also essential to a huge range of products including steel, formed using a coal-derived material called coke, and plastic, which is produced by refining and processing crude oil and gas.

Fossil fuels are by far the biggest contributors to climate change. When burned to power our modern lives, they emit carbon dioxide (CO2) into Earth's atmosphere, trapping heat and causing temperatures to rise.

With 2025 officially one of the warmest years on record, the impact of these emissions is being felt around the world. Hotter temperatures are causing polar ice caps to melt and creating the conditions for extreme weather events — such as floods, drought, wildfires and storms — to become more intense and frequent.

Scientists stress the need to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to avoid unleashing the most catastrophic impacts of climate change. That was laid out in the 2015 Paris Agreement. Currently, there are 194 parties to the agreement, but progress has been too slow, and overall emissions continue to rise.

Three years after countries agreed at the UN climate conference in Dubai COP28 to transition away from coal, oil and gas. After the previous COP in Brazil failed to reach a consensus on a concrete plan, Brazil has now presented a roadmap aimed at turning that promise into national plans.

"It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable," United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said.

Oliver Glasner has played down the significance of his warning to Nottingham Forest’s squad after their defeat at Brentford has had the desired impact.

The Austrian said last weekend there would be “no compromises” and insisted his players have to fully buy into his philosophy.

Speaking this week, he said: “I didn’t attack anyone directly. We share that we want to be successful and win games. It was not a problem.

“It was much louder outside than I felt it was inside. This is just how I see a relationship has to be. Let’s talk about things if we don’t like things.

“If you never say anything in your relationship with your wife or children, then they will never know. Then I can’t blame somebody because if they don’t know, how can you expect things to change?

“We are now in a society where criticism or the way I talk is negative, but the intention was positive and to change to get better results so that we can all have a better life.”

Gianluigi Donnarumma, who has made three errors leading to goals this season, “recognises that he has made some mistakes,” Enzo Maresca said this week, “but at the same time recognises that he has made some great saves”.

The City manager added: “It is quite easy with him because he recognises any mistake immediately. I’ve spoken to him about it, but I didn’t feel the need to be so deep with him because he already knows and recognises that he has made some mistakes.”

Asked about City players adapting to his philosophy, Maresca said: “I can see my playing style just by working every day with them, but we can still improve many things.

“We know exactly what we are doing well and what we need to improve. It is just a matter of time.”

Elsewhere this afternoon, Martin Odegaard has broken the deadlock at the Emirates to give Arsenal a 1-0 lead over Hull City.

Victory would take Mikel Arteta’s side six points clear of City at the top of the table before this evening’s contest at the City Ground.

Glasner has made two changes to his Forest team following defeat at Brentford last weekend, with Yates and Munoz replacing Ndoye and Aina.

Is this the day the xG gods reward Nottingham Forest? Oliver Glasner’s team sit 19th having won one game all season, but there is no doubt that their performances have been significantly better than results and they might need their luck to turn against Man City team full of firepower.

Despite all of the positive indicators in Forest’s underlying data, Glasner caused some alarm with his comments after last weekend’s defeat at Brentford.

The Austrian said: “We have to accept it’s not good enough. If we lose four of the last five games, it’s not good enough. And that’s why for me, it’s now time that we change things, that I change things, and that’s what I will do.

I will tell [the players] what we want to do, what we have to do, and if the players buy in, I think we can have a turnaround, and if not, the sixth manager [since the start of last season] will come in.”

Glasner has happy memories of playing City, beating them in the 2025 FA Cup final with Crystal Palace, but his Forest reign is in urgent need of a signature victory and performance.

#1058. Helsinki puts trust at the heart of its smart-city model

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Benjamin Plackett is a science journalist based in London.

Helsinki Central Library Oodi is just one example of a building in the Finnish capital that uses real-time data to optimize energy efficiency.Credit: Sergei Gapon/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images

Urban planners — and curious residents — can go online and click on almost any building in Helsinki to see a host of details including its age, height, heating source and estimated energy use. The information sits in the various maps that make up Helsinki 3D, an open-data digital twin of the city built by the City of Helsinki from aerial photographs, light and detection laser scanning (LiDAR) surveys, housing registers and geographical data. The project’s Energy and Climate Atlas estimates heating demand for nearly every building, models how it would change in response to different climate conditions and calculates the solar-panel potential across every roof and wall in the Finnish capital.

Helsinki’s technical prowess in these kinds of projects is underpinned by a substantial research base; the city is ranked 100th among the world’s top 200 cities in the Nature Index, with particular strength in health sciences (ranked 69th), biological sciences (80th) and Earth and environmental sciences (83rd). It produced 55% of Finland’s total Share in 2025, a ratio that is among the highest for cities in the overall top 200.

The city has treated itself as a laboratory, too. Kalasatama, a brownfield site in the harbour district of Helsinki, has been designated as an urban testbed for researchers, city officials and companies to try out novel urban infrastructure ideas.

Helsinki’s Nordic climate is also an advantage when it comes to handling the large amounts of data involved with smart cities. Cooler air reduces the energy needed to chill large data centres and the excess warmth created by such facilities is redirected to residents using heat pumps. One of the largest data-centre operators that publishes its waste heat recovery data says it recovers up to 90% of its waste heat, which is fed into the district heating network — enough to warm 14,000 two-room apartments.

One of Helsinki’s most distinct smart-city features is the way it uses data.

“We have to be responsible when we use AI. We must do it in a transparent way,” says Pasi Rautio, a service manager for the City of Helsinki’s AI and optimization unit.

The city’s AI register, for example, allows residents to keep tabs on AI projects the city’s government is running. It shows what data are being used and why, and offers the opportunity for public feedback.

#1055. Jensen Huang: Spy row, affairs leave Nvidia without its rockstar CEO

Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia into the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, is stepping down as CEO over extramarital affairs. DW examines how losing its figurehead will affect the firm and the US-China AI race.

Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future as reports emerged of other extramarital affairs — this time with employees.

In a statement issued on Thursday, the world's most valuable chip supplier said Huang was resigning as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately.

The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.

Under Nvidia's bylaws, Huang can be removed "with or without cause" by a majority vote of its 11 directors.

The New York Times first reported that the 63-year-old Huang had an affair with a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him.

Later Thursday, Reuters news agency alleged an intimate relationship between Huang and a second employee, citing unidentified sources.

Those revelations emerged just three days after Huang admitted a relationship with a Chinese woman, whom United States intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The woman, Alice Huang — no relation — is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that runs artificial intelligence (AI) data centers across Southeast Asia and is a major client of Nvidia.

The US government is investigating the startup on suspicion that it secretly sent some of its Nvidia chips to China, violating Washington's curbs on high-end semiconductors.

Those advanced Nvidia processors ‌are ​used to train and run the large AI models behind chatbots and other generative AI products.

Megaspeed denies the allegations and on Thursday pledged to cooperate with US investigators.  Huang, the alleged spy, has been barred from entering Singapore and Taiwan — a key chipmaking island.

While Nvidia's board backed its CEO after the first scandal emerged, market watchers believe the second caused too much reputational damage to one of the world's top three companies by market value.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Huang doesn't believe in formal succession planning, so with little notice, Nvidia appointed CFO Kress as interim CEO.

Bloomberg reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board is working with advisers to identify potential permanent successors.

Kress, other senior Nvidia executives and members of Huang's own family have been mooted as replacements. The family members include his daughter Madison, a senior director of product marketing, and his son Spencer, who currently works in the firm's robotics division.

Rumors also abound over a longer-term solution. On India's CNBC-TV18, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld from the Yale School of Management floated former Apple CEO Tim Cook and ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt.

US President Donald Trump also backed Cook on social media, writing: "A Legend replaces a Legend."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The scandals have certainly hit Nvidia's market value. Since the first extramarital affair emerged on Sunday, the chipmaker's market capitalization has fallen by well over $600 billion to $4.2 trillion.

Nvidia shares were down more than 9% in premarket trading Thursday, after dropping by 10% earlier this week. Some analysts expect the stock price to struggle in the short term.

Nvidia stock hit all-time highs just a month ago as US technology giants continued to announce billions in spending on AI infrastructure.

Demand for Nvidia's advanced chips is so high, however, that many market analysts expect little impact on near-term sales.

"While Jensen [Huang] is the heart and lungs of the Nvidia story…the company and its leading-edge GPU technology will go on and [his departure] does not change the entrenched position Nvidia has in the AI Revolution chip arms race," said Dan Ives, a partner, senior managing director and tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, a US-based merchant bank

Analysts see the biggest long-term risk in strategy and execution. After all, Huang was the leader who picked which ideas Nvidia should bet heavily on and got the whole company behind them.

His sudden exit is also seen as highly disruptive to the chip designer's strong relationships with AI hyperscalers, Taiwanese chip producer TSMC and foreign governments — especially China.

Huang was Nvidia's main lobbyist on US chip export rules and persuaded US President Donald Trump to ease some curbs on China last year.

Huang is often called a rockstar CEO for his leather jackets instead of suits.

Like Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, he was also seen as a key-person risk as Nvidia’s public image, strategic direction and technical decisions became closely tied to him.

Huang steered the company for more than three decades and was also respected for his hands-on involvement in product architecture and engineering decisions.

He also insisted on a flat management structure, with around 60 executives reporting directly to him.

Huang has run the company so tightly around his own technical judgment and product decisions that investors may have little sense of how it would function without him.

At the same time, Nvidia is no longer the startup Huang founded in 1993. The company has built deep expertise in chip design and software, creating a durable moat that helps protect its huge profits, which topped $120.1 billion last year.

Some analysts argue that its central role in the AI hardware buildout makes it less dependent on Huang’s day-to-day input.

China is quickly playing catch-up with the US in the global race for AI dominance.

While Chinese AI models have lagged behind the likes of ChatGPT and Claude, recent updates from DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot have closed much of the gap on benchmark tests and often beat US rivals on cost and speed.

Beijing is also investing heavily in domestic chips and data centers to reduce reliance on US hardware.

The US has curbed exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips.

However, this move has only slowed the pace of China's AI ambitions.

Reuters reported Thursday that Chinese AI firms are now trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centers outside China, amid fears the US could further tighten restrictions on advanced chips.

Also Thursday, Beijing accused the US of using the Nvidia spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological "blockade" on China.

The issue is likely to dominate talks next week between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen in southern China.

#1053. Iranian activist and Nobel Peace Prize winner Narges Mohammadi shares her story in memoir

Written and smuggled out of prison, the 2023 Nobel Prize laureate's memoir reveals the cost of defying Iran's regime and fighting for freedom.

As PEN International marks Imprisoned Writer Day on November 15, a memoir by 2023 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi stands as a powerful act of resistance against authoritarian regimes.

"A Woman Never Stops Fighting — My Struggle for Freedom, Democracy and Human Rights in Iran," was recently published in German and is set to be released in English in September 2027.

The autobiography "portrays how Narges actually became the woman she is today — and it also reveals the price she had to pay to become that woman," Mariam Claren, spokesperson for the Narges Mohammadi Foundation Germany told DW.

Mohammadi wrote the autobiography in prison: "She was constantly writing," says Claren, whose own mother, activist Nahid Taghavi, shared a cell with Mohammadi for two and a half years, in Iran's notorious Evin prison. "Then, in 2020, Narges was forcibly moved to another prison. All her documents were gone. And she had to start all over."

But she managed to rewrite it all, and her texts were smuggled out of prison in fragments by fellow prisoners and visitors who risked their own safety.

In her memoir, Mohammadi recounts pivotal moments in her life, including her childhood and youth, how she started taking action against gender discrimination, political repression, the death penalty and human rights abuses, and the personal and emotional toll of her activism.

The human rights activist has been sentenced to a combined total of more than 44 years in prison and 154 lashes. For more than a decade, she has been separated from her twin children, who are now 19 years old and live in exile in France for their own protection.

Born on April 21, 1972, in Zanjan, Iran, Narges Mohammadi became politically active while studying in physics at Imam Khomeini University of Qazvin in the 1990s.

In "A Woman Never Stops Fighting," she describes how she started mountain climbing as a student, and organized mixed-gender groups dedicated to mountaineering — a controversial initiative at the time. She also helped establish an independent student organization and advocated for political reform. Her activities led to repeated harassment and arrests by authorities.

She began her journalism career in 1996, writing about Iran's student and women's movements. As her public profile grew, she became increasingly involved in Iran's civil society and human rights community.

In 1998, she married political activist Taghi Rahmani. The couple's twins, Ali and Kiana, were born in 2006.

Over the course of her career, Mohammadi worked with some of Iran's most prominent human rights organizations and became a leading figure in the Defenders of Human Rights Centre, founded by 2003 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Shirin Ebadi.

She played a key role in initiatives promoting free elections, peace and the abolition of the death penalty, especially for juvenile offenders. She also helped establish organizations supporting political prisoners and advocating for women's rights.

Her first major prison sentence related to her human rights activities came in 2011. It marked the beginning of a cycle of arrests and prosecutions that would define much of her adult life.

In her memoir, she describes an arrest that took place in front of her young children. At one point during her imprisonment, she lost the right to call them for several months.

She also details the brutal treatment she experienced in prison, with constant interrogations, beatings and denial of medical care.

Another central focus of her activism is denouncing the psychological effects of solitary confinement, which she had previously documented with fellow inmates in her book and documentary project "White Torture."

"When someone is subjected to physical torture, the scars, blood and infections — dreadful as they may be — serve as visible witnesses," she writes in her memoir. But, she adds, "when someone is subjected to psychological torture, no visible traces remain, and the victim cannot justify the trauma — neither to themselves nor to others. In fact, it becomes virtually impossible to even accept that one has been tortured at all, which causes the suffering to continue indefinitely."

"This is also the goal of solitary confinement: to bring the imprisoned person to the very edge of nothingness — to strip them of their identity and of everything that makes them human," she writes.

Through her relentless campaigning against executions and state violence, she helped bring these issues to the forefront of public debate among Iranian activists.

International recognition of her work culminated in October 2023 when she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for "for her fight against the oppression of women in Iran and her fight to promote human rights and freedom for all."

As Mohammadi was unable to attend the ceremony because she remained imprisoned in Tehran's Evin Prison, the award was accepted on her behalf by her teenage twins, who delivered her message to the world.

Following the Nobel Prize, Iranian authorities continued to pursue new legal cases against her, restrict her communications and intensify pressure on her from prison.

She became the target of a systematic smear campaign, including widespread defamation, gender-based harassment and explicit death threats.

"We are firmly convinced that the Islamic Republic of Iran has deployed its cyber army — which is the second-largest, after Russia's — to this end," says Claren of the Narges Mohammadi Foundation. Conspiracy theorists even started claiming she might be working for the regime, she adds: "And what is truly terrible about this is that when a lie is repeated over and over again and spread over the course of years, it eventually leads even ordinary people to start believing it."

In late 2024, following surgery, Mohammadi was granted a temporary medical release. Doctors warned at the time that a return to prison could seriously endanger her health.

Nevertheless, Mohammadi was brutally arrested again in December 2025, while attending a memorial ceremony for Khosrow Alikordi, a lawyer and human rights activist who died in suspicious circumstances.

In prison, she was held in solitary confinement for an extended period and her health continued to deteriorate, Claren reports. But "thanks to a public campaign, she has now been granted what is known as an interruption of detention for medical reasons."

But "that doesn't mean she is free," adds Claren, who notes that she still suffers from serious health problems — as do many Iranians who have been tortured in prison.

In February, an Iranian court ordered additional prison sentences for Mohammadi, along with a travel ban.

Mohammadi lives in constant fear of having to return to prison any day, notes Claren, and "this all comes with the pressure to which Iranian civil society — including, of course, people like Narges — is currently subjected, with questions like: Will Trump launch an attack, yes or no? Will there be another war?"

Despite this uncertainty, Mohammadi continues her activism. Her international profile also helps her supporters keep addressing publicly the issue of human rights in Iran in the public eye, says Claren: "It is incredibly important that, alongside the individual Narges Mohammadi, the focus also remains consistently on the struggle of the people in Iran for freedom, dignity, and fundamental rights — for the right to sing and dance."

#1050. Why Oliver Glasner is taking on the Nottingham Forest dressing room: The frustrations behind 'English-speakers' rant, key players up for sale in January, his tick-list for transfer targets and the Morgan Gibbs-White conundrum

Published: 12:00 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 12:00 EST, 26 November 2026

Nottingham Forest's restless players have already seen off two managers in the past 12 months but now Oliver Glasner believes he will beat them at their own game.

The strength of feeling within the squad helped force Ange Postecoglou and Sean Dyche out of the door after 39 and 114 days respectively and after a dodgy start to his reign, there were probably one or two who thought Glasner would go the same way.

No Premier League boss is ever immune to results and another run of defeats would make Glasner vulnerable. Forest have won two games all season and are above the relegation zone only on goal difference, ahead of Friday night’s clash with Chelsea at the City Ground.

But as things stand, Glasner has the backing of Forest owner Evangelos Marinakis to make the changes he needs – and that could be bad news for some senior players.

Daily Mail Sport examines the power struggle bubbling away at the City Ground...

Nottingham Forest's restless players have already seen off two managers in the past 12 months but now Oliver Glasner believes he will beat them at their own game

Glasner took aim at some players' lack of English skills in light of a disappointing start to the season that sees his side hovering outside the relegation zone on goal difference alone

Early in his reign, Mikel Arteta stamped his authority on Arsenal, moving on high-profile players like Mesut Ozil, Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang and Alexandre Lacazette.

Even at the start of his managerial career, Arteta would not compromise and was prepared to clash with big names if they would not match his standards. Arteta knew what he wanted and if he had to fight some stars to get it, all well and good. Now look where Arsenal are today.

It will not have escaped Glasner that despite their success, the champions work ferociously hard and seem to carry no outsized egos or sense of entitlement. That may worry certain Forest players.

This is the source of Glasner’s remarks about players not learning English – but that is not his only issue with the squad. He wants time-keeping to be sharper, training sessions to be slicker.

It is thought Forest will listen to offers for Ola Aina and Callum Hudson-Odoi in January, while Ibrahim Sangare has work to do to force his way into Glasner’s plans. Hudson-Odoi and Aina are influential figures in the dressing room and Sangare is highly respected, too. Is Glasner trying to smash this power base in order to cement his own?

Glasner wants to add more athleticism and physicality to his squad in January as he has been alarmed at how Forest have been outmuscled in certain games. As things stand, he has the mandate to shape things his way after a three-hour meeting with Marinakis in London this week.

It will not be easy. Glasner can change some things yet a fair number of this squad are on their fifth manager. They were outstanding for a season under Nuno Espirito Santo in 2024-25 but they have drifted since. It still feels a long way until January and that is why – more than ever – Glasner needs the captain on board...

Glasner wants players' time-keeping to be sharper and training sessions to be slicker

A glance at the numbers shows that Morgan Gibbs-White is having an outstanding season. Not bad for a player in a team above the relegation zone thanks only to goal difference.

Albeit from a smaller sample size, Gibbs-White is performing better than last term on all of these metrics (per 90 minutes). Last season, he finished with 15 league goals and four assists. England boss Thomas Tuchel appreciates the underlying numbers and after leaving Gibbs-White out of his World Cup squad, has brought him back into the fold this autumn.

Gibbs-White is Forest’s most talented player and it is believed he would have accepted a move away from the club last summer, after watching Elliot Anderson join Manchester City.

There was tentative interest from Chelsea but Gibbs-White wanted to play in the Champions League and it is thought he would have been open to a move to Manchester United. The 26-year-old’s boyhood idol was Wayne Rooney – but the Old Trafford club have never truly pushed for him. That may change if Bruno Fernandes leaves next summer.

Gibbs-White is the highest-paid player in Forest's history and is halfway through a three-year deal. Few expect him to be at the club for life and if he moves in summer 2027, nobody will be surprised.

Yet there is a feeling in the game that Gibbs-White’s body language can count against him at times. When team-mates are not quite on his wavelength, Gibbs-White is often quick to show his frustration. If he creates a chance that a colleague misses, it is a similar story.

Morgan Gibbs-White's numbers are very impressive this season. At times, the same can't be said for his body language

It is difficult to be rational in the heat of battle but could Gibbs-White try to stop these issues at source? At Forest, each part of the team – defenders, midfielders and forwards – have discussions before matches. That would be the perfect opportunity for Gibbs-White to guide others, to explain his thinking and where they should be when he has the ball in certain areas.

Because unless the player is Diego Maradona or Lionel Messi, top clubs do not look at talent alone before making signings. Gibbs-White has the tools to play for an elite team but in other aspects, there may still be some work to do.

Glasner and his staff hope Forest’s best player can inspire others, as he has in the past. Club skipper Ryan Yates returned to the starting XI for the last two matches and if he loses his place against Chelsea, Gibbs-White would logically regain the armband. #1046. Could lack of money sink TFFF rainforest fund before it even launches?

The TFFF rainforest fund aims to make forest conservation more profitable than deforestation. But a lack of money may prevent it from getting off the ground.

The world's tropical forests play a vital role in slowing global heating and preserving biodiversity, storing climate-damaging carbon dioxide and providing a home for an extremely large number of species — when they're intact.

More than 140 countries committed to halting global deforestation by the end of the decade at the 2021 UN climate change conference in Glasgow, but five years later logging continues.

In 2024, over 8 million hectares (19 million acres) of forest were lost. And since 1990, nearly 490 million hectares of forest have been wiped out.

More recently, the trend has shifted in the opposite direction. Deforestation in the Amazon region of Brazil decreased by 41% from August 2025 through 2026 to reach its lowest rate since records began.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

To ensure lasting protection, the Tropical Forest Forever Facility was launched in 2025 at the COP30 climate conference in Belem, Brazil.

Because rainforests are so important for the world, the idea behind the fund was to give money to the countries where they are located to help them preserve and protect these ecosystems.

So far, these countries have made more profit through deforestation — for example, by mining natural resources on rainforest land or farming the area.

Starting in 2027, the TFFF is expected to generate the funds needed for rainforest conservation, in part via contributions from various countries. By the end of this year, a total of $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in government capital is due to flow into the fund, mainly in the form of low-interest loans.

In addition, the TFFF is expected to issue bonds to private investors, such as banks and investment firms, to raise additional funds — initially totaling about $40 billion.

Going forward, the plan is for governments to contribute a total of $25 billion to the pot, and for private donors to contribute $100 billion. The fund will then invest this money in international financial markets with the aim of generating profits.

Private investors who purchase TFFF bonds can expect to earn about 5% interest per bond per year, said Felix Finkbeiner, the founder of the German environmental organization Plant-for-the-Planet, where he is responsible for forest conservation and advocacy.

"Private investors' capital is very well protected," Finkbeiner said, adding that any losses the TFFF might incur on the capital markets — for example, if the price of its bonds should fall — would be offset by government funds.

About 2.7% of the TFFF's profits would be set aside for countries with tropical forests.

Countries would receive $4 per year for every hectare of forest that they preserve instead of chopping down. At least 20% of these funds must be allocated to Indigenous peoples and local communities.

According to calculations by the TFFF Watch website, an independent platform launched by Plant-for-the-Planet to track investments, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for example, would receive about $333 million for its 2024 forest stock under this system.

Finkbeiner said the subsidies would be paid only for intact ecosystems and not for timber plantations, with forest areas and their condition mapped and assessed using satellite imagery. Though it can sometimes be difficult to identify plantations accurately on satellite photos, he said, the technology has improved significantly over the last decade.

That means any NGO or external party with access to the satellite data can check the condition of the region, providing further oversight. If forest areas are cleared or damaged, money is deducted from the total.

Another safeguard: If countries don't use the TFFF funds for rainforest conservation, their payments could be frozen for the next few years.

The TFFF is supposed to invest, whenever possible, in government bonds issued by emerging and developing countries. Above all, the idea is not to invest in projects that harm the climate — such as those linked to oil, gas, or coal investments.

The TFFF concept has received plenty of support from environmental organizations, in part because it gives countries in the Global South significantly more sovereignty than traditional forms of development financing.

"For example, if the government of Ghana wants to protect its rainforest today, it usually asks the World Bank for financial assistance — and then the World Bank in [Washington] DC decides whether Ghana is allowed to do so," Finkbeiner said.

The TFFF fund is also designed to be immune to donor countries' backing out in the event of a change in government, for example. Once a contribution is made, the money remains in the fund for 40 years before being paid back.

Continuing protection is also an incentive for countries receiving money from the fund. "When a new government comes into power that wants to cut back a little on climate protection, they will realize: We'll get more money if we protect the rainforest," said Finkbeiner.

For the rainforest fund to actually get off the ground, a total of $10 billion in seed capital must be raised by the end of 2026. So far, the confirmed pledges from countries, NGOs and foundations total only $7.9 billion.

Eight countries have expressed a willingness to contribute so far, including Brazil, Indonesia, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.

Norway, with a pledge of $3 billion, is the largest would-be donor. However, the government in Oslo is willing to honor its commitment only if the agreed-upon total amount is in place by the end of the year.

"This deadline isn't set in stone, but otherwise the Norwegian government will have real trouble getting it through parliament," Finkbeiner said.

Germany's commitment must also still be approved by the parliament. The German government has pledged about €1 billion to the TFFF starting in 2027, to be paid out over 10 years.

Other countries are also considering investing in the TFFF, including Canada, China, South Korea and the United Arab Emirates.

Philanthropic organizations have pledged $88 million to the fund so far, including $73 million announced this week during the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. Finkbeiner remains upbeat.

"Promises like that always come at the last minute," he said. "I'm very optimistic that we'll secure more commitments at the COP — and in the course of December — and that we'll then reach that $10 billion."

This article was originally written in German.

#1043. Daily briefing: A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Source: P. J. Klasse et al. Nature Rev. Microbiol. 23, 734–752 (2025).

By harnessing potent antibodies that can vanquish diverse viral strains, scientists are closing in on one of the most elusive goals in biomedical research: a vaccine for HIV. This year, several research teams described vaccination strategies that triggered the production of these broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) in monkeys, and precursors to bnAbs in people, suggesting that an effective vaccine is possible. But devastating cuts to US funding for HIV research have left some efforts in limbo.

The world is closer than it has ever been to an effective HIV vaccine. It also has a drug capable of preventing infections: the long-acting injectable drug lenacapavir, which could avert an estimated one-third of new HIV infections in Africa if given to just 5% of adults. Now is the time for funders to ramp up investment, not cut it back, argues a Nature editorial.

Reference: UNAIDS & Gates Foundation report

Pregnancy causes drastic changes to the brain, but we know little about them because of past worries about the safety of scanning pregnant people. Now, researchers are working to fill that void by collecting scans from first- and second-time mothers and analysing thousands of archived brain scans acquired during routine clinical care. The work, presented last week at the US Society for Neuroscience annual meeting, could help to explain maternal mental-health conditions such as postpartum depression.

‘General purpose’ artificial-intelligence tools such as OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude are impressing researchers with their emerging biology skills, including protein design and structure prediction. In some tests, these models have even outperformed those designed specifically for biology tasks and trained on vast troves of protein-sequence data. Some scientists predict that generalist AI tools could eventually catch up with, or surpass, blockbuster models such as AlphaFold. Others suggest these new abilities could be the result of regurgitating training data, rather than advanced learning.

As I write, the United States army is preparing to detonate around 4.4 tonnes of unstable lead azide, a chemical used to make munitions, at an ammunition plant in Iowa. “It's essentially a lead bomb,” says occupational and environmental health researcher Patrick O’Shaughnessy. “Now it's a matter of how much gets ejected out of the bunker.” Academic researchers have banded together to gather independent public data about the plume of toxic lead dust that is expected to spread over the area.

Figure 1 | Position verification. a, To check the location of a party called the prover, two verifiers each send a random bit (a challenge), which are timed to reach the location simultaneously. The prover combines the bits and returns the answer. Because no signal travels faster than light, a prompt reply shows that the prover is at the location. b, However, if two adversaries, one near each verifier, copy a challenge and pass it to each other, they can answer in time even though nobody is at the claimed location. c, In Kavuri and colleagues’ scheme, one verifier generates two entangled photons, keeping one and sending the other to the prover. Both verifiers then transmit classical challenges. The prover uses the challenges to determine how to measure its photon and returns the result, while the first verifier measures the other photon. If the prover’s result arrives in time and the two measurements pass a statistical check (a Bell test), the transmitted photon must have been measured at the claimed location.

“Banks, power grids and satellite-navigation systems all depend on knowing where a request or a signal comes from, yet claims about location are notoriously easy to fake,” notes physicist Davide Bacco. Now researchers have outlined an experiment in which the position of a distant party is certified using quantum entanglement.

In a, two verifiers send random bits (challenges) timed to reach the claimed location simultaneously. The prover combines them and replies. Because signals cannot travel faster than light, a prompt response verifies the prover’s location. But two adversaries (b) can defeat this test by exchanging the challenges and responding in time. In (c), a verifier also sends one of two entangled photons, which are inexorably linked in a way that can be proven using a statistical check (a Bell test). If the prover’s result arrives inside the time window imposed by the speed of light and the photons pass the Bell test, the prover must be inside the target region. (Nature | 9 min read)

Chemist George Whitesides made landmark contributions to many fields, including patterning surfaces with molecules — a technique that enabled ‘lab on a chip’ diagnostic devices — advances in nanotechnology and more. He prided himself on switching research interests often, telling students, “If somebody else is working on something, don’t work on it.” In traditional chemistry departments, “there’s often a lot of pressure to stay in your lane, and he made it okay not to”, says polymer scientist Joseph DeSimone. “In fact, he made it exciting not to.” Whitesides has died, aged 87.

Read Whitesides’s guide to writing a scientific paper in a special issue of Advanced Materials that celebrated his 65th birthday.

Some mental disorders seem to take different forms in different places, writes mental-illness researcher Alexander Pereira. “Even depression – arguably the most common psychiatric condition in the world – seems to look strikingly different depending on when and where it appears,” he writes — with bodily symptoms, such as fatigue, prevalent in China, and psychological symptoms, such as low self-esteem, more common in the West. Pereira argues that our ability to adapt to our social environment might significantly shape the internal mechanisms of mental health.

Changing location — even just walking through a doorway — can signal to our brains that work is over and it’s time to relax, says cognitive scientist Joan Ongchoco. (BBC Future | 11 min read)

Reference: Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology paper

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03879-2

The stunning geological formation was buried in the 1886 eruption of Mt Tarawera, but it will never be forgotten.

#1038. Germany's Nmecha won't repeat controversial goal celebration

Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp has said midfielder Felix Nmecha will not repeat a goal celebration that sparked controversy over the past week. Germany are set to face Serbia and the Netherlands in the Nations League.

With the controversy sparked by Felix Nmecha's celebrations after his goals in Dortmund's 2-1 win over Elfersberg last weekend, the subject was always going to be top of reporters' minds when Germany coach Jürgen Klopp faced reporters ahead of Friday's match against Serbia.

Nmecha celebrated the goals by mimicking taking a crown off his head and kneeling to place it on the ground.

This was understood by many to be a nod to a Ballers in God (BIG) campaign called "The King's Return."

BIG, a Christian group for footballers, has said it aims to "demonstrate love and respect towards everyone," but critics claim it discriminates against the queer and transexual people. The discourse generated by the celebration did not go unnoticed by the Germany boss.

​Klopp told reporters in Belgrade on Thursday evening, that the 26-year-old Nmecha had assured him that he meant no harm by his actions.

"Last weekend I ​saw Felix score two great goals and saw the celebration and then the gesture. I thought nothing of it at the time, but then it all kicked off," he said.

"As the controversy escalated, I started looking into the details of the subject and trying to form a clear picture of it.

"I confronted him with all the things you (reporters) might have confronted him with. He told me that it had nothing to do with that at all, and that he loves all people and does not discriminate against anyone."

He then said that Nmecha had agreed not to repeat the celebration.

In Friday's match, Klopp's goal will be to keep alive Germany's chances of reaching the Nations League quarterfinals with a win over Serbia. Germany are third in Group A2 with 5 points, trailing the Netherlands and Greece, who both have 8. Serbia, who Germany beat 2-0 in Munich last month, are still without a win.

"We feel well prepared," Klopp said, adding that his team were committed to earning "a final" for the last group last group game on Monday in Berlin against the Netherlands.

Klopp also expressed his disappointment that only a few thousand Serbian children would be admitted to the stadium due to a spectator ban. Originally, the game was to be played behind closed doors after Serbia was sanctioned for racist and discriminatory behavior by its fans. However, a clause in the UEFA rules allows a selected group of guests to attend. Now children under 15 accompanied by teachers or football coaches are expected to be at the match.

"We're expecting some 5,000 guests," a spokesman for the Serbian FA told the DPA news agency. The stadium's capacity is 55,000. The German FA has been allocated just 50 tickets for its fans.
